Dr. Bush went on:
If we were to enter a war tomorrow it would be a tough slugging match, much the same sort of tough slugging match from which we recently emerged, with some improvement of weapons in various categories it is true, and with new features, but nevertheless a rigorous trial of strength that would test the staying power and fighting ability of this country to the utmost in every department of its activity. It would be a war in which we would need to gird ourselves by all means for sustained rigorous effort. It would be a war in which we would need men and armies as well as implements with which they could fight.
That is the view of one of the world's outstanding experts.
A second and similar point is that our own exercises and experience confirm the view held, I believe, by most authorities, that in the immediate future any attack on North America would be diversionary, designed to panic the people of this continent into putting a disproportionate amount of effort into passive local defence.
A third point is that a potential aggressor, if it had atomic weapons at all, would use them on targets of the greatest strategical importance, and it is very unlikely that in the near future such an aggressor would use any such weapons he had on many targets in Canada. In this short-term period Canada is almost certainly'going to be neither the Belgium nor the Bikini of the next war.
These statements are made in the light of all the knowledge available and on the best possible advice. What must be realized, if we are to play our role sensibly, is that there is neither an easy nor sudden solution to the problem of our national defence. There is no easy guarantee of security; it cannot be bought for a billion a year. Rather it must be patiently and anxiously striven for. The signs point ahead to countries like Canada having to face a long period of great uncertainty. We cannot live with our problems day by day without clear heads and stout hearts and mutual support.
One danger is that the Soviet union, without any genuine change of attitude, may suddenly appear to be seeking co-operation in a deliberate effort to induce the people of North America and of the western union to say, :'Why bother about all this defence business." A second danger is that we should come to regard war as inevitable. A third danger is that we should commit our future resources to expenditures, equipment and plans that will be out of date when needed.
Role of Canada's forces. Because we live alongside the United States, it is often thought that our role should be the same. Canadians are prone to expect our country to spend or 
arm on a corresponding scale and to act in much the same way as the United States, just because we have so many common interests at. heart. But in fact the difference of size makes many of the problems, and still more the possible course of action, of the itwo countries very different. The Unitedi States is the world's greatest power, with all the consequences that result from this fact in every corner of the world. Canada has shown in two world wars her capacity to make great, even amazing, contributions to victory; during and since the war we made contributions to the conditions of peace, proportionately as great as or greater than any other country; but the fact is that by themselves our forces could never deter the Russians, nor in a general conflict could they deliver a knock-out blow. What we want are forces which can defend Canada and enable us to play such part as parliament and the people may support in any efforts for common defence with other countries.
Against this background it is now possible to set down Canada's present defence aims and objectives. They are: (1) to provide the force estimated to be necessary to defend Canada against any sudden direct attack that could be or is likely to be directed against it in the near future; (2) to provide the operational and administrative staffs, equipment, training personnel and reserve organization which would be capable of expansion as rapidly as necessary to meet any need; and (3) to work out with other free nations plans for joint defence based on self-help and mutual aid as part of a combined effort to preserve peace, and to restrain aggression.
In the United Kingdom a white paper on defence issued last February summarized their objective:
His Majesty's government are determined to maintain balanced forces adequate to fulfil their responsibilities in peace and to serve as a nucleus of expansion in war.
In Canada we are planning so that the three services and our great agricultural and industrial resources each has the means to play its role to meet the needs of the particular time. All these forces must work as a team, together and with others.
The business of defence has become very complicated. You may remember how Switzerland prided herself, and rightly, on her citizen army, when each man after his year of service brought home his uniform, his rifle and his cartridge belt, ready to serve his country again. But this cannot be done .by a modern army. Today only about ten per cent of the fighting effectives of any modern force are riflemen, and even those riflemen now use six other weapons. But how would

Supply-National Defence
a man bring home one-sixth of a tank, one-fifth of a radar set, and so on? The same question may be asked about nations. No one country can be fully enough armed to meet and master the onslaught of modern war; each has its fraction of power to contribute to the common defence.
Defence today is a complex business which must be balanced, integrated and planned. Our plans are being made now for up to five and even ten years ahead, with changes provided for to meet expected developments. We are trying to ensure that everything we do today will be a sound basis on which to make future developments of any kind and at any time. Our plans are flexible. If, as we hope, western union grows into a North Atlantic security understanding, this may involve further modifications, just as in the more distant future there might be modifications resulting from any more general arrangement under the charter of the united nations which was agreed to by parliament.
For the short term, however, our roles are clear and evident. At sea our role would largely consist of guarding the lines of communication as the Royal Canadian Navy did so well during the last war. Canadian ships once again would be called upon to provide the vital protection for troops and supplies travelling the northern seas our sailors know so well.
Recognizing the importance to us of the northern waters, an exercise will take place with the new arcticized aircraft carrier Magnificent, two destroyers and a tanker going north into Hudson strait this summer. The destroyers will go on to Churchill, the first Canadian warships ever to enter Hudson bay. We are also constructing for the navy a large modern icebreaker. During this last year the navy carried out training cruises totalling 91.366 miles. Fourteen fighting ships were in commission and twenty-two in reserve, with 58 auxiliaries in commission and 67 in reserve, most of these auxiliary vessels being small craft.
The active army, in the first place, is to include a brigade group or later such additional force as may be considered necessary, trained and equipped to deal with any diversionary attack. Secondly, the active army is to provide the administrative and training staff-the cadre of officers, N.C.O.'s and tradesmen-to train the reserve army and with it form the nucleus for as large a force as Canada may need.
In the air, only three countries are at present able to maintain an effective strategic bombing force. We are, however, maintaining one permanent and two auxiliary bomber squadrons
In this way we will keep abreast of modern trends and development in the art of bombing. Our main peacetime task will be to supply interceptor fighter squadrons and ground forces necessary to deal with attacks on Canadian territory. These will be valuable units from which to draw the nucleus of larger forces should the situation demand it. The R.C.A.F. will activate two regular fighter squadrons during the next twelve months. The operations of these units will require the activation of additional bases in Quebec and New Brunswick, located at Chatham, Mont Joli, and Bagotville. In this way we will fill in our chain of bases across Canada, and will be able to get experience in operating conditions in all parts of the country.
During the year we completed taking delivery of 85 Vampires, 30 Mustangs, 23 North Stars, 20 Firefly IV's, 27 Seafuries, 3 Sikorsky Helicopters, 3 Chipmunks, and 36 Austers, bringing the total number of planes of all types to something well over 1,000. An idea of the cost of present-day defence equipment may be gained from the cost of these 237 planes at today's prices, not less than 835,000,000. Work on the "Chinook" jet engine and the airframe of the two-seater fighter is being accelerated to bring this plane into production in Canada as speedily as possible should it test out satisfactorily. This powerful jet plane is specially designed to meet Canadian conditions and is the first fighting plane to be designed and made in Canada. Work on new planes, modifications and overhaul was provided for a number of Canadian industries to enable their essential organizations to be kept together.
In recognition of the increasing importance of the air this year for the first time we shall be spending more on the air force and fleet air arm than on either the navy or army.
Form and amount of estimates. The form of this year's estimates shows a number of changes from last year. Considerably more detail is given and there is a new provision for current year commitments as an addition to the amount to be appropriated.
Putting together all the relevant items of defence in the main estimates there is authority for an appropriation of 8232,408,239.95, and for a commitment of $20 million, or a total of 8252,408.239.95 for 1948-49, where last year there was an appropriation of 8239,960,617.40. While the final figures are not in, it is estimated that the amount expended in the year 1947-48 will be 8196 million.
As I pointed out, our plans are subject to constant examination and development. The supplementary estimates which were put before you yesterday will seek an additional
Supply-National Defence

$15 million in cash appropriations for the air force and further authority to commit, of $17238.578 for the three services for 1948-49 and $31,505,959 for navy and air force in future years. The supplementary estimates will also seek an additional $3,800,000 for defence research to accelerate development work on the jet engine and frame. Further supple-mentaries will be sought later if necessary to carry on the program as planned or as it may be altered to meet changing circumstances.
Putting these various items together, the total cash appropriations sought for defence for 1948-49 are $251,208,239.95, with authority to commit for an additional $37,238,378 this year and $59,938,028 for future years, which will permit an increase in defence activity generally greatly in excess of the increase in cash expenditure over last year of $55,000,000 or approximately 28 per cent.
As you will see from the figures I gave earlier, we now have 85 per cent of the active forces at present authorized. These targets have not in any substantial way limited our recruits or our efforts this year. As we near the target, however, that might happen. We shall continue to recruit above the announced target figures, using the additional men as they are obtained to activate more ships, to bring the brigade group nearer to strength and to re-activate several air force stations. The government will do everything it feels to be required to meet the defence needs of Canada as these may change from time to time.
Civilian activities. Service personnel-officers and men and nursing sisters-when they become full-time servants of their country do not cease to be members of the community. That has been dramatically brought home this year. The work of the three services in connection with civil activities included the heroic rescue of Canon Turner; the photographing of 111,043 square miles of territory by vertical camera and 293,000 miles by tri-camera to provide maps for mining and other civilian as well as military purposes; assisting dominion observatory officials to re-locate the magnetic pole; putting a weather ship near Greenland; search and rescue work at sea by the R.C.A.F.; flying on fifty operations, twenty-three of which resulted in the rescue of persons in distress; the construction of Bailey bridges by reserve units of the Royal Canadian Engineers; maintenance of the northwest highway system, the northwest staging route and the northwest territories and Yukon telegraph system; continued work on winter living and testing winter equipment at Churchill, and the highly creditable job by active and reserve units of the navy, army and air force in fighting

the flood conditions and providing relief in British Columbia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. These all meant more in service to the country than our forces have been able to do before in peacetime.
Conclusion. During this last year it was my privilege to visit most of the establishments of the navy, army and air force across Canada. There I met not only officers and men, but also members of the civilian community. With all of them I discussed the relationship of the forces to the community. I had one conviction. The closer the civilian comes to the armed forces, the more inclined he is to like them and to give them his approval and support. I imagine that the people of the Fraser valley will say the same thing. On that account we have encouraged visits, arranged for open-house occasions, such as visits to ships and camps and air force day, and done everything possible to bring the services and civilians closer together. In sport there was a good example in the Olympic champions, the R.C.A.F. Flyers, who on and off the ice gave a good account of themselves and their country.
There can be no doubt as to the quality of the forces we are building. It is essential, not only that our forces be trained for duty, but also that their own people, the citizens of this country, be proud of them, respect and admire their efficiency, and realize that even when the headlines are not threatening and the march of armed feet is silent, the defence forces of this country are continuing to do their work in maintaining peace.
Two wars and a world-wide depression have shown that we cannot dissociate ourselves from the security of others. We shall continue to work with other nations to preserve peace and to create the conditions in which peace can be preserved, at home and abroad. We are building defence forces in accord with what any self-respecting Canadian would regard as our need and our responsibility.

When we begin to examine these various items we find that the total figure is not quite as impressive as it might seem to indicate. On referring to these details, I find that there are many items which could hardly be described as contributing directly to the defence of the country. For instance, there

I could not help smiling when the .minister referred to the fact that the necessity of providing this accommodation had been recognized by his predecessor, because it came to my memory how-I ithink it was in 1945 or 1946-in commenting on the estimates at that time, I had emphasized the necessity of providing good quarters for the permanent force of our country. At that time the minister definitely pooh-poohed the idea and said that that could still wait. However, cognizance has been taken of the necessity and it is right that we should provide this accommodation.
Under various headings of acquisition, construction, purchases, maintenance, repairs and rentals of property which are given in the details, I notice that there is a sum of approximately $40,000,000. I notice that it was given in a press release made by the minister some time ago. There are no material changes in that.
As the minister said, this way of presenting the estimates is novel. I think we shall have to ask him how he proposes to deal with one major item, namely, item 243. If everybody rises in his place and discusses first of all the

Turning to policy, one would expect to find the foreign policy of the nation reflected in the defence estimates, as the minister rightly said it would be. It was not very long ago that the Secretary of State for External Affairs stated in this 'house:
The best guarantee of peace today is the creation and preservation by the nations of the free world.-under the leadership of Great Britain, the United States and France-of an overwhelming preponderance of force over any adversary or combination of adversaries.
These are proud words. I suggest that they were proud words which the minister used in his memorandum, and we must examine these estimates to see whether they "were proud words supported by something more than mere words, or whether they were just idle vapour-ings which would really carry no weight in the country.
I do not think I should be over-simplifying the case if I said that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and also the Minister of National Defence, in his statement today, would lead the country to believe that we were ready and willing for any emergency. Perhaps some doubt might be expressed as to the willingness, because of the uncertainty and the indecision which was voiced a few days ago and, I think, repeated by the minister today, in the statement that Canada would not be willing to join in any defence pact, in so far as western Europe wTas concerned, unless the United States were also in that pact. All I can say in that respect is that it is a very good thing for Canada, and a very good thing for this world, that w7e did not wait for the United States in 1914 or in 1939.
We must examine the figures which have been given to us and see whether they support the statement of our readiness. The three military objectives which the minister announced this afternoon were-I jotted them down briefly-one, to provide against a sudden attack; two, to provide the staff necessary to enable a rapid expansion of our forces, and, three, to join in the making of joint plans to ensure and preserve the peace of the world. I have no comments to make upon the third objective. The minister has explained that

there is a planning staff, consisting of officers of experience, who are studying continually the plans which are necessary for the preservation of world peace, and no doubt to consider also the other two items. But when I come to examine the figures which have been given to us at various times regarding the availability or the readiness to meet a sudden attack I fear that I am not satisfied, and I cannot help saying I believe that to meet a sudden attack at the present time Canada is impotent.
Today we have been given certain figures regarding strength. I am not able to remember all these figures-I do not know that they are very important-but earlier this session questions were put on the order paper as to the strength of the forces at that time, and the strength given as at March of this year was considerably less than the figures w'hich were given today. Naturally, recruits are coming in. But remember that a man who has joined the forces since March of this year can hardly be considered thoroughly trained and ready to take his place in the field. Therefore, in order to meet a sudden emergency, I think it would be wiser to take the figures of last March than the figures given today, which include the latest joined recruit.
As regards the Royal Canadian Navy, it was [DOT] shown that there were 6,782, while in the naval reserve there were 3,247. We know there are not enough personnel in the Royal Canadian Navy to provide full ships' complements for the vessels we have.
When we return to the army, the total number given in March was 15,409. We have a reserve army of 28,743. The minister in his statement gave numbers slightly in excess of that. About 1,000 would have joined the active force since then, and the reserve forces have increased to 35,000.
The minister gave target figures to which he referred. Frankly, I do not understand those, because they were different from the limited establishments which he imposed in 1947. A further reduction seems to have been made in the targets at which we are now aiming. I would, however, bring this fact to the attention of the committee. While we may have 15,000 or 16,000 men in the active army, we must remember that only a very small proportion of these can be termed combat troops; that the large majority of these men are employed on- administrative work around headquarters, driving lorries, acting as clerks and so forth; and that even in the combat regiments there are always personnel who have to be employed on administrative duties.
As I said earlier, I have not the full details regarding the correspondence which may have

been exchanged between the Premier of British Columbia and this government; yet it is significant that the combat units of British Columbia and the prairie provinces had' to be pretty well drained of active personnel in order to provide approximately 2,000 men who were fighting in the flooded areas.
But the point I wish to emphasize as strongly as I can is that we must not be misled by the idea that 15,000 or 16,000 men are readily available.
When we pass on from there we come to the Royal Canadian Air Force. There were in March some 11,636; I believe the number has now increased to 12,296. I think that was the figure the minister gave. But also in March there were, according to the figure he gave, only 1,282 actual flying personnel. That gives some idea of the large number of men it is necessary to employ on administrative duty in order to provide a small fighting force in the air; and if that figure of 1,282 which was given to us as being correct in March is still approximately correct, that gives us some idea of the extent of the force we have available now to meet a sudden attack.
If one wishes to see what opportunities there are of expanding that force rapidly, I suggest that we take the figures for March. I find that there are only 692 personnel in the Royal Canadian Air Force auxiliary squadrons. That is not a very hopeful indication that the small number of active air force personnel could be rapidly expanded. I am sure I am correct in saying that these 692 are certainly not all flying personnel. There would be only a limited proportion of these flying, because the squadrons would have to have a certain number of ground personnel as well.
It is not only numbers that we have to consider. We have to consider the efficiency of these forces. If we are to rely entirely on the active army, there are, as I have shown, only very small numbers; but I believe that by recruiting at large now we could get many men-I believe the minister said many hundreds of thousands of men-who were trained along the lines of 1944 and who would no doubt come back and join the colours. As soon as they could be welded into units they would be available, but that would take time.
I suggest that, although we may have that large number of men who were trained in the war, they could not be as readily organized as they were in 1939, because our reserve army units have not had the same opportunities of training as units that were available prior to the outbreak of world war II.
I have here a publication known as the Canadian Army Journal, issued under the authority of the chief of the general staff,
which was sent to hon. members with the compliments of the Minister of National Defence. With reference to training which was carried out in my own province, I notice that the composite camp which was held at Chilliwack for reserve force units of British Columbia, other than artillery, engineers, armoured regiments and the Canadian Scottish regiment, lasted for a week at that centre. That embraces infantry units in the city of Vancouver, and so on, and they were able to send into camp a total of fifteen officers and ninety-nine other ranks.
Rather naively the officer who wrote this article said that the administration of this camp was no problem. I should not think it would be. Turning to the training of other units, the Canadian Scottish regiment-I ask hon. members to realize that this is a regiment, a full battalion-went into camp with thirteen officers, fifteen warrant officers and men, and sixteen rank and file, making a total of forty-four.
The report states that it was not possible to carry out the regular training, but all ranks received general military training and the program culminated in a platoon exercise.
I bring this up only to let this committee know that there is a considerable question in my mind as to the readiness of our defence forces to meet this sudden attack to which the minister refers.
Then I come to two even worse cases than that, and I am sorry that I have to quote British Columbia figures exclusively because I have not them for elsewhere. Two regiments in the interior, the Ninth Reconnaissance regiment, an armoured unit which one might expect to be sent early in order to meet any sudden attack, trained exactly three officers and nine other ranks; while the Rocky Mountain Rangers trained three officers and thirteen other ranks. That is the condition of the units in British Columbia; and from conversations I have had. I have reason to believe that it is materially worse in other parts of this country. It is a fact, as disclosed by what the minister was saying, that the emphasis has been placed on the training of officers, noncommissioned officers and specialists at certain schools of instruction. That is all very well; but we must not, ostrich-like, believe that we have in the active army units which could be made readily available, and we certainly have not such units in the reserve army.
When we refer to the reserve army we must not be misled by that name. Usually "reserves" give the indication that they are men who have passed through a period of training and are held in reserve readily available to fill the ranks of some unit which is in

existence. That is not so in Canada. We never used to refer to our non-permanent units as reserve units. They are separate units, largely composed of only partly trained personnel.
We have a naval force about half the size of the force which was indicated in 1946. We have, as hon. members know, the Magnificent, on loan from the British navy, which has just joined us in the last few weeks. We have one cruiser capable of sailing the high seas; the other is in reserve. We have no complement of men ready to man her immediately. Half our destroyers are in reserve, and it would take time to bring in the naval reserves and fit them into their places in the ship's company in order that those destroyers might take their place in the event of a sudden emergency. If we are to guard our sea lanes, as was suggested, we are short of trained personnel in the fleet air arm, and it is to be remembered that we have no submarines. While we may have sent a few officers and ratings to the Royal Navy for training, we have nothing like experienced crews to man any submarine, should that necessity arise.
I have already referred to the air arm. I am pleased to hear the minister say that more emphasis is to be placed on the air arm than has been shown in the past, because I have firm ideas with regard to its necessity and importance. While it may be possible for us to raise a force that we might be able to send across the seas or use for the defence of Canada, we must recognize the fact that at best this will take two or three months; and a force which requires two or three months at best to raise the first nucleus is not a force which is capable of dealing with a sudden attack which might come now or at any time in the near future.
I think the failure, and it is a failure, on the part of this government to provide that force is mainly because the government has consistently refused to recognize our changed position in the general make-up of the world organization for defence and the changed geographical position of Canada in view of the new inventions which have appeared on the defence scene in the last few' years. I cannot help feeling that there is a certain wilful blindness to the lessons which should have been learned from Pearl Harbor, Czechoslovakia, Poland and many other places where such attacks were launched. Campaigns are won by nations doing the impossible, in exactly the same way as battles are W'on by units and individuals accomplishing the impossible.

I will cite only one instance. It was declared impossible for an expeditionary force from Great Britain to land on the coast of France during this war until a port had been captured. Our raid at Dieppe showed the great hazards and risks entailed in the capture of a port. What did General Montgomery and General Eisenhower do? They built a port- it was called "Operation Mulberry"-and towed it across the English channel. By this means they had a ready-made port from which to launch their offensive against Germany.
I issue a serious warning against basing one's plans on the fact that certain things are not possible. I do not believe it is likely that a push-button war could be initiated bj? any country in the immediate future. But I am equally convinced that countries may spring a strategic or tactical surprise which, w'hile not going to the length of push-buttor warfare, might find us in an extremely unfortunate position. I feel that this blindness which has been adopted has had a tendency to make us adhere to time-honoured, though perhaps time-worn formations. I do not know that w-e are alone in that respect.
I should like to read a paragraph from a report published by the air policy commission of the President of the United States, under the chairmanship of Thomas K. Finletter. It is entitled "Survival in the Air Age", and is an official publication of the United States. This is what the report states, at page 30:
We view with great anxiety the pressures from many sides directed towards the maintenance of yesterday's establishment to fight tomorrow's war; of unwillingness to discard the old and take on the new; of a determination to advance the interest of a segment at the sacrifice of the 'body as a whole. All this is understandable. For it comes in large part from loyalty of each service to its traditions. But we can no longer afford the waste it involves.
I feel that we are trying to build on the old formations of days gone by, which were designed to meet circumstances entirely different from those of today, defence organizations to meet situations which were never present in the time of our forefathers but which are definite realities today. I do not like all this talk about Canada's defence forces being so stream-lined, that everything has been so nicely integrated. It is easy to talk like that; but at the invitation of the Minister of National Defence, which I greatly appreciated, an opportunity was given hon. members to visit the main ordnance stores here in Ottawa. They are up to date in many respects, but time-honoured and time-worn traditions still prevail. We saw men using new and modern

equipment to pile the stores. Then we came to a barrier, and the ordnance officer said, "Now I must hand you over to an officer of the army medical corps, who will show you how the stores there are .piled." We went on and came to another barrier, where we were handed over to an officer of the army dental corps, who showed us how the stores were piled by his corps. This was all in the one building, but of course it was necessary to have the building divided into compartments, because the ordnance corps reported to the master general of the ordnance and the quartermaster general, while the army medical corps and the army dental corps reported to the adjutant general. And who could expect a man accustomed to piling bundles of puttees to be able to pile bundles of bandages? I hope that situation has been changed. I am sure the minister is working in that direction. I just say these things to show that we have not yet reached our goal, and I am sure the minister agrees that much work remains to be done in order to do so. I should add that naval personnel were working there, and perhaps naval stores also were issued.
Then 'I want to refer to one statement made by the minister which I do not find supported by the estimates. He said more money was being spent this year on the air force than on either of the other two sendees. I do not think that is correct, according to the figures contained in the estimates. As I total them, we are spending $80,000,000 on the air force, whereas the total being spent on the army is $95,241,000.
I have emphasized the importance of the air force. As a soldier I would welcome greater emphasis being placed on our air arm, because I believe it is of primary importance. We must find a means of stopping the enemy bomber from reaching its target. That is the first requirement as far as the defence of Canada is concerned. To do that we must not only have an interceptor force readily available; we must also have the means of obtaining early warning. A week or so ago I had an opportunity to attend the industrial fair in Toronto. I do not know whether the minister attended personally, but I know some of his officers were there. At that fair three radar sets were displayed; and I regret to say that, while Canada was far ahead in the radar field during
the war, the British equipment demonstrated,
I think by a group of firms known as Cosser, was far ahead of the radar sets made by our Commercial Corporation or Arsenals Limited.
I hope we are not losing ground in that allimportant field; but the difference in definition was so marked that a layman could see how far we were behind the British sets, and it really was not funny.
Finally I want to say just one word about the important subject of civil defence. I believe some nebulous plans are being made, though they have not gone beyond the blueprint stage. I would urge the importance of developing the civil defence of this country, because if w'e are ever threatened the civilian population of our cities may have to take the brunt of the enemy's onslaught just as much as the actual fighting forces. To mention one very small field, just as an example of the direction in which preparation for civil defence might be attempted, I would refer to the co-ordinating and unifying of fire-fighting forces throughout the country. As it is now, in the province of Ontario you have in some towns fire departments which are incapable of rendering assistance to firedighting detachments in other towns only a few miles away.
I have perhaps over-emphasized lack of numbers, or have devoted more attention to that point than I should, because I am not sure that the shortage of numbers is the main shortage we are experiencing. I feel that shortage of equipment and shortage of the means of producing equipment in this country, particularly air force equipment, is one of our greatest handicaps; and that supporting industry which, as the minister said, turned this country into one of the arsenals of democracy during the last war, seems to have been allowed to slip back, so that it cannot play its all-important part in the national defence of this country.

I am one of those who was pleased this afternoon to hear the Minister of National Defence refer to the close connection of his department with the Department of External Affairs; and I am also pleased to see the minister back in the house supported, as he was at one time, by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. That in itself is significant, to see the minister's statement listened to with interest by those who have perhaps the most responsible positions in Canada's government. That has not happened for many a long month in this house.
I hope the minister's colleagues took note of some of the things which were missing

from his statement. I refer in particular to one paragraph:
Canada has a strong interest in the standardization of training and operational techniques, communications procedure, classification and handling of stores, industrial standards and the adoption of common weapons and equipment. Discussions have been taking place with the United States towards this end. Similar discussions have been carried on with the United Kingdom. Progress is being made.
He reports in four words the most important aspect of the whole defence picture- "Progress is being made". Canada is expected to be satisfied, and hon. members are likewise expected to be satisfied with the words, "Progress is being made". I ask him today: What progress?
Referring again to this statement, may I point out the extreme fallacy in the arrangement of these different things he has mentioned. Standardization; of training, operational techniques and the like all depend upon the adoption of common weapons and equipment, which is placed at the end of this list. All these other things will fall into their proper slots as soon as we start to use common weapons and equipment. It is as simple as that., I hope the attention of the minister's advisers will be called to that one reference which I make at the beginning of these remarks.
I go back to the matter of co-operation with the United States and the United Kingdom. AVe have noted the purchase for Canada of eighty-five Vampire fighters which, I understand, are first-class operational aircraft, the finest perhaps in the world today in that field. Although we hear many reports, we still know that Britain continues to make a workable, able and efficient aircraft, and that she is some years in advance of other countries in the world in the production of jet engines for aircraft.
The pity seems to be that these aircraft had to be shipped to us from the United Kingdom for assembly here in Canada, and that we are without the means to produce them in our own factories by Canadian labour. There, it seems to me, is the essential weakness in purchasing our equipment abroad. If the producers of these aircraft could be persuaded to make them in Canada, and to continue to keep their production up to date, in Canadian aircraft factories, we would be able to have a source of supply here at home of a modern air weapon, and in that respect achieve standardization with the United Kingdom.
On the other hand, I notice that we bought twenty-three Mustang fighter aircraft from the United States. These aircraft and the spare 
parts for them can be obtained on this continent. That is a step forward, although I regret that they are not produced here in Canada by Canadian labour, so that our industrial machine could maintain production in the event of any difficulty, and the additional supplies and spares could be obtained from our own industrial machine.
I should like now to make a suggestion to the minister in both these fields. If we are to co-operate with the United States and the United Kingdom, Canada has scarcely the financial resources sufficient to keep its air force equipped with modern weapons by buying them from either the United States or the United Kingdom. \Are already have a tremendous adverse balance of trade with the United States. If we are to standardize our equipment and if we must buy our equipment from them we shall never rid ourselves of that adverse financial balance. Therefore, if we would seek to standardize, and if they will accept co-operation, it w-ill be necessary for the American aircraft industry or the American defence department to let contracts in Canada. They could let contracts for aircraft with which we could equip our forces, and deliver to them any surplus quantities for the equipment of their own forces with one particular type of machine.
To my mind this is essential, because I believe Canada's air defence should be based upon North American industry and equipment. It means that our government should adopt a policy of integrating our air equipment with that of the United States forces. The joint defence board should be asked immediately to decide the respective defence roles of the Royal Canadian Air Force and the United States air force.
Our Canadian representatives would be well advised to adopt for the present a policy which would be primarily defensive, because of our size and our inability adequately to undertake more than one specialized role in the defence of the continent. When these decisions have been taken our government should arrange for the mass production in Canada of the type of aircraft selected for Canadian defence in a program of North American cooperation. As I have said, part of this production could be absorbed by the United States forces.
When this suggestion is made to our cousins south of the border there will probably be a distinctly negative reaction. That is not surprising, because their aircraft industry has been hit as hard as, if not harder than our own Canadian industry, and has need of sustenance by means of new contracts. I understand from reliable sources, however,

that about 65 per cent to 70 per cent of the content of any aircraft built in Canada is of United States origin. That is, Canadian aircraft manufacturers must buy from United States sources up to 70 per cent of the value of the aircraft they are making. So it can be seen at once that the American aircraft industry will not be greatly damaged by the suggestion I am about to make, and our own process of co-operation and standardization will be immeasurably assisted.
I rise frequently in the house to advance the idea of adequate air defence, for the simple reason that I believe that, through the continued development of our air force, we can protect this continent. We can do something more; we can protect the peace of the world. I say this, because in history we have had two examples where the peace of the world has been maintained by strong military forces. The first to which I would refer was the Roman empire, which was based upon the Roman legions. They kept the peace by keeping at bay the barbarians who threatened the frontiers of their empire. That was known as the Pax Romana.
The second example is the Pax Britannica, which followed Nelson's great victory over Napoleon's fleet at Trafalgar. It was based upon the British navy, a navy which devoted itself to clearing the sea lanes of the world of pirates and privateers in the navies of those countries which did not wish to trade peacefully.
In this new era of world development, many legions are too few and fleets of ships are too slow to cover the space and distances necessary to secure our western civilization. The only disciplined arm of national defence which can be devoted economically to peace is our air force. If that single thought can be projected beyond any service or national prejudice we can accomplish a Pax Americana based on air supremacy.
That is the thought which I should like to leave with this committee today. I urge the minister to ask his defence advisers to sit down again with the United States members of the joint defence board to see if some degree of standardization and co-operation cannot be worked out.
On April 16 I asked the minister some questions about joint defence. I noted at that time that the house of representatives of the United States had voted 417 to 5 to spend over $3,000,000,000 on air defence in order to raise their air force to 70 groups for the protection and security of their country. I went on to ask him if he was endeavouring to arrive at any joint agreement by which Canada might assist in the over-all defence of this continent. The minister replied that it would be almost inconceivable for the United States to request any action by us or to suggest that we should co-operate with them. To me that was a foolish reply. We do not need to fear our friends, and surely we can work with them. It seems to me that it is too bad if that effort has broken down and1 we are to be a party to letting the situation remain as it is.
Earlier I commented on the fact that the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State for External Affairs were in the chamber while the minister wa3 speaking. At this point I should' like to place on the record a statement by General Eisenhower, contained in his official report of February 7, 1948, as follows:
I believe we have finally learned that national defence is not the exclusive property and con- . cern of men in uniform, but the responsibility as well of labour, management, agriculture, industry and every group that goes to make up the national complex.
And a little later on, he said:
The United States army supports the theory that air power occupies a dominant position in modern warfare.
Whenever I have an opportunity I rise in this house to put forward, not old worn-out ideas but new ones, to make constructive suggestions to the minister in order to try to achieve the thing we all want, namely, the security of our country by the .proper defensive equipping of our armed forces. I have finished for this afternoon except to quote an old Hindu proverb, which reads:
A man without a stick will be bitten even by a sheep.
We want Canada to have a stick. We want these international wolves who may be appearing in sheep's clothing at the present time to know we have a stick. We know a great many who have suffered from their attentions in the past now realize that they have long fangs.

The position of the Minister of National Defence is not an easy one at this time, for many reasons. The danger of war is here and we must try to prepare for an emergency without adding to that danger. Canada has never been a military country, although our exploits in wars that we have engaged in have been considerable, when one considers our population and our resources. If we are to prepare adequately for an emergency I assume that we should have some knowledge of how great that emergency may be. That is something we do not know, nor do we know from what direction or at w-hat time it may come.
I gather that there has been some difficulty in getting men for the various branches of the armed services on a voluntary basis. If we were to try to get them on any other basis I am satisfied that it would only make the world situation worse and add to our own difficulties. I was glad to hear the minister say our defence policy is closely associated with our external policy. I am satisfied that, no matter what happens, at some time we shall have to get down to world co-operation. We must work for that with those who are willing to work with us, and we must offer every inducement to those who will not work with us, to come in with us and work for peace.
We are now planning the defences of Canada which I imagine every hon. member feels is necessary. It is amazing that those who are so keen on planning for national defence should be so much opposed to economic and social planning, not only on a national but on an international basis. Unless we do that we shall never have freedom from the fear of aggression. As a matter of fact, I think one comes before the other. If we are to get the world into a position where we can avoid war we can do so only by getting the world together and planning for the improvement of the economic and social conditions of mankind. I hope that we shall never leave that out of the picture.
I read an article the other day, but I cannot remember the name of the periodical which contained it. The author was showing that in the matter of its natural resources the United States was not in a position now to put the same effort into a war as it did in the last one, simply because of the lack of these natural resources which are today called upon in a great war such as the last two. These wars are the wasters, not only of our human resources but of our natural resources which are needed for economic development. We should not-I am glad that the minister did not do so-in our preparation to defend ourselves, consider that war is inevitable. Today there are strong forces working for peace

as well as those forces which we believe are working for war, or at least working for that kind of economic chaos which naturally leads to war.
I do not know that there is anything further I can say or need to say on this matter, except I hope that the government will do everything within its power while it is preparing the defence of this country, associating ourselves with other countries that are of like mind, to build up the economic and social conditions of the world wherever we can, because I am satisfied that that is the only way in which peace can be maintained.

I am not quite clear whether the hon. member suggests that the Department of National Defence has anything to do with this man. I say that, because it would not appear that the Department of National Defence had anything whatever to do with him.

It may be that the Department of National Defence does not have anything to do with the case. I am not exactly sure, but I cannot see how in the world the Department of National Defence can conduct its affairs in preparation for world war III effectively, unless the Department of Veterans Affairs is taking proper care of the people who fought in world war II.

I thank the minister. I have little else to say. I will say no more regarding this particular matter.
May I conclude, however, by saying that I am well pleased with the minister. I have been watching him closely as the man upon whom the fate of Canada and perhaps of the British empire hangs or will hang in the future. Naturally, being a citizen of both these units, I am deeply concerned. I believe the country's military affairs are in good hands, and I assure the minister that we will do all we can in our group to support him in the arduous task to which he has been called. At the same time, whenever we see anything in his department that calls for criticism we will not hesitate to bring the matter to his attention with all the emphasis we may find it possible to summon.

The minister has made a lengthy and important statement of defence policy in introducing his estimates this afternoon. Certainly, to those of us who for some years have strenuously advocated that there should be regular statements and discussion of defence policy, the minister's practice, last year and again this year, is a source of satisfaction, and we should like to express our agreement with the course he has followed. But inasmuch as the statement is so important, we would not be discharging our part of the duty that rests upon us all if we let it go without some comment.
Supply-National Defence

Critical analysis has already been made by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey), but there are other features of the statement which require some analysis and comment because, although it is a source of great satisfaction that we have had the statement, and are not left with the feeling that defence matters are being treated inadequately in that respect, I feel that some aspects of the policy outlined in the statement are inadequate. It is the inadequacy of the policy that I should like to examine for a few minutes before going on to the other question that I wish to discuss, namely the position of our reserve force.
In analysing the statement the minister made this afternoon, and statements he has made on other occasions in this house and in speeches outside the house, one can only gain the impression that the present assumption of the department is that the next war will probably be fought on the same terms as the last one; that is to say, any war which might be thrust upon us in the near future wall be fought on the same basis as the war which was concluded just three years ago.
There seem to be two parts to that assumption. There are some signs of planning or willingness to plan* for a war which might be thrust upon us in ten or fifteen years' time-what might be called a deliberate war. I think, however, it is safe to assert that the assumption is that what is regarded as an accidental war, or what the department calls an accidental war, which might come within the next two or three years, shall we say, will be fought on exactly the same general basis, the same general plan of campaign, as the war we have just finished.
That, to my mind, is a basically unsound assumption, and any plans for Canada's defence based upon that assumption are unsound and inadequate. It seems to me that there are many factors which when analysed should convince us that any war, whether it comes in the next one, two or three years, or in fifteen or twenty years' time, will be fought on a basis vastly different from that on which the war that started in 1939 was fought. It follows, therefore, that Canada's defence policy should consist of much more than plans for what I believe is called a deliberate war, a war in the fairly distant future.
With regard to an immediate or accidental war, I suggest that if war came at any time in the near future it would be an accident as far as we are concerned, although we can depend upon it that in the minds of those nations which would be the aggressors there would be

nothing accidental about it. It would come because they thought that by a sudden war they could obtain an initial advantage which would make it a short war.
So long as we continue to base our plans for defence on the assumption that war, if it came, would be fought on the same basis as the last w'ar; so long as our plans are predicated on that idea, I suggest that any war in the next two or three years would in fact be a short one because our preparations would be totally inadequate.
That means that even the short-range defence policy must be so designed as to take into account the progress made in weapons, armaments and tactics during and since the last war. Here I would refer to the minister's statement of this afternoon. He said that "a second danger is that we should come to regard war as inevitable." That, of course, is quite true; it is a mental attitude that must be resisted. But he went on to say that "a third danger is that we should commit our future resources to expenditures, equipment and plans that will be out of date when needed."
Of course that is a danger; nevertheless it is a fact which we must face. We- must have some equipment and some plans, and we must make some expenditures to meet the possibility of war in the immediate future and, as I have said, to meet the fact that war when it comes will be fought on a vastly different basis from the last one. What seems to be happening at the present time is that the department is so much concerned not to build weapons and prepare plans which will be out of date ten or fifteen years from now that it may fall into the trap of having virtually no plans and no weapons adequate to meet an immediate war. If the assumption of the department that an immediate war would be fought on the same terms as the last one were correct, the danger I see would be minimized. But certain as I am that an immediate war would be fought on a different basis, the weakness in the department's analysis becomes evident, and that is the main weakness in the defence policy being at present pursued.
Another point which shows the weakness to which the policy exposes us is contained in another part of the minister's statement where he analyses Canada's present defence aims and objectives. He lays down as a first objective:
To provide the force estimated to be necessary to defend Canada against any sudden direct attack that could be or is likely to be directed against it in the near future.
This objective, to my mind, if we accept it -and I think it is a sound objective that should be and will be accepted-obviously imposes on us the necessity of having forces

Supply-National Defence
adequate to meet that sudden attack. That attack may come in the immediate future- in one, two or three years. On the other hand, if we are so obsessed' with the idea of not having out-of-date plans and equipment that we have virtually no plans, equipment and forces at all for the near future, then obviously we shall not be in a position to meet that danger and to achieve our first objective.
The first requirement in order to meet that first objective is obviously that we should have sufficient forces with which to meet the danger; and because of our peculiar position, that involves the necessity of strong and prepared reserves capable of immediate mobilization and formation into an effective fighting force. Here again, when we analyse the figures with regard to our reserves, as I shall do in a moment, it seems to me that we can see the weakness in the department's plans for meeting the immediate war.
In further analysis of this weakness, I should like to refer the committee to the minister's statement where he discusses the possibility of a push-button war. I agree with him to some extent that, to talk of a pushbutton war and to concentrate on that as an immediate likelihood, might lead1 us into dangers and wrong courses of action. On the other hand, I think the minister and the department have been led into discounting altogether the possibility of such a war in the immediate future, and into going so far as to say in effect that in the immediate future there will be no substantial change in the weapons and tactics from those with which we started the war just concluded.
I wish to refer to a passage of the statement the minister made this afternoon in which he said:
Theoretically-
And I should like to emphasize that word. -it is possible for missiles to be guided by various devices to their destination hundreds, if not thousands, of miles away.
It is not only theoretically possible; it is actually possible. It was being done at the end of the last war. V-l rockets were used for one and a half years before the end of the last war. V-2's or guided missiles were being used at the end of the last war. Those who have had practical experience in the matter and know the over-all picture, have said in no uncertain terms, that had it not been for the fact that by 1945 we had attained land and air superiority over the enemy so that we could overrun his territory and take over his bases, thus preventing him from using those guided missiles, the outcome of the war might have been much different from what 5849-368
it was. Certainly the fate of London and of other cities in England would have been horrible to contemplate. The point is, of course, that these missiles or weapons were in existence, were being used at the end of the last war and will be used1 in larger numbers, and in more perfectly developed form, at the beginning of any war in the future.
On ranges of about 200 miles.
I think that is an entirely unwarranted assumption when one remembers-
I admit they were used. But I asked if it is not true that they were used at the end of the war on ranges up to about 200 miles?

That is not my impression. I should not care to engage in an argument on that basis, but my recollection is that the ranges were considerably more than 200 miles. But we must remember this fact. Russia is the country which took over that portion of Germany in which experiments on those weapons were being carried on. It certainly would be a false assumption to suppose that Russia, as well as ourselves, has refrained from any further development of guided missiles.
The minister went on in that portion of his remarks to say this:
But these new developments have not in fact yet been carried to the point where it is possible for them to change the character of war or make out of date either existing concepts or existing equipment.
That statement is, I think, typical of the weakness in policy which I have been pointing out. Those weapons were changing the character of war. They were making out of date existing equipment. I am not saying that the department is totally blind to the importance of research or of adapting our methods to meet possible new weapons and equipment. It would be foolish for me to make that statement categorically. But I suggest that the frame of mind which would lead to the formulation and expression of such a statement as that, indicates that at the moment we are not preparing our defence plans to meet an immediate war in any realistic fashion; that we are not bearing in mind that the character of warfare is being changed every day; and that we are in fact making no effective plans to meet the next war which, whenever it comes, I am certain will be characterized by a totally new, much more rapid, and in many respects totally unexpected, form of attack.
The whole tenor of the minister's statement in that regard indicates the belief in the minds of the department that we shall again have an

minister gave a reason this afternoon why in his view we could not have a large and highly trained reserve force. In my opinion that reason is nothing short of laughable.
I shall read the passage from his remarks where he compared the situation today with the situation as it existed in Switzerland where, as he said, the Swiss reservist used to go home with his rifle, and have it and the ammunition with him at home. The minister said he was in fact a highly trained and organized reservist of the army of those days. Then he proceeded to say that today's equipment is so complicated and so ponderous that we cannot have an adequate reserve force.
I am sure my hon. friend would not wish to misquote me. I did not say anything of the kind whatsoever.

I certainly do not wish to misquote the minister. At the moment I do not seem to be able to lay my band on the passage where he made his statement. I believe, however, that I can state fairly that the minister did give that outline of the Swiss reserve force, and said this sort of force would not be of any use today in view of the complications in our equipment and weapons. He said you cannot take home one-sixth of a tank or one-fifth of radar machine, or any thing similar to that.
Of course you cannot take home one-sixth of a tank or one-fifth of any other machine and say you have a proper reserve force. But that is not to say that we cannot train our men in the use of tanks, that we cannot train them in the use of radar. Certainly a large part of our defence force today consists of other than riflemen. Only riflemen can take their rifles home with them. One cannot, of course, take home a piece of an aeroplane, if he is in the air force.
I have succeeded in finding in the minister's remarks at page 21 of his prepared text:
Today only about 10 per cent of the fighting effectives of any modern force are riflemen, and even those riflemen now use six other weapons. But how would a man bring home one-sixth of a tank, one-fifth of a radar set, and so on?
The argument simply does not apply, because in order to have training in tanks, radar, the handling of aircraft and any other line of military training required by our forces, one does not have to bring the equipment home at night. He goes down to train with that equipment, and uses it during the period of training. The force is organized into a well-trained and formulated reserve unit.
As the hon. member for Nanaimo pointed out today, we have practically no such trained units in Canada at the present time. He gave figures of the number of men who have

gone to camp, and indicated that in one rifle battalion there were only thirty-three. In that respect I refer to Colonel Goforth's requirement that a real reservist is a well-trained reinforcement.
In addition to trained men, to be adequate a reserve force must have organization; the units as well as the formation must be complete. As Colonel Goforth pointed out, our reserves must be given an allotted place in those units and formations, so that in the event of sudden attack we may have a reserve force capable of being sent out, capable of rapid mobilization-not leisurely, but quickly -and ready to meet an immediate threat.
In conclusion, I should like to read from the white paper on defence published last year under the authority of the present Minister of National Defence. It is based largely on the speech he made in the house on July 9, 1947, when introducing his defence estimates. Speaking about the reserve force, he is quoted at page 11 as follows:
We can never express too warmly the appreciation this country owes to the officers, N.C.O.'s and men and their civilian friends who by their voluntary support maintained our reserve forces through the difficult period of the years between the wars.
In outlining the defence objectives last year, he mentioned these two as numbers 5 and 6:
5.	Development of reserve forces of an age and with educational and physical standards *and training approximating those of the active forces and who will in time be capable of entering speedily on active service at sea, on land or in the air.
6.	Provision for reserve forces of the most modern training methods, administration and training officers, and adequate equipment.
In view of the figures given this afternoon showing the serious disproportion between the men actually on strength in the reserves and the authorized strengths, and in view of the figures given by the hon. member for Nanaimo as to the appallingly low number of men in our reserve units who went to the various training camps, it can be safely and certainly said that neither of these objectives is being carried out or fulfilled, nor are we fulfilling the debt of gratitude outlined by the minister himself.
I realize that in the remarks I have made as to the necessity for an adequately trained and organized reserve force there is a fundamental problem which must be faced. We have not the men in the forces at the moment and our program is deficient in that respect. The reasons are numerous and certainly they are highly controversial.

Supply-National Defence
First, I think we should reject entirely and I think the minister should reject entirely the words which he uttered in this house on March 16 with respect to "good progress" being made in connection with recruitment and organization of the armed forces. I suggest that that is not a fact. Then we must contemplate more far-reaching steps than are at present being taken to bring our reserves up to strength. We -must face the problem and find a means of solution. The problem involves a recasting of our outlook and of our whole appreciation of defence needs at the moment. It involves our having the courage to resort to the measures necessary to fulfil our plans and fill up our ranks.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate that the minister has recently undergone an operation and is not feeling too well, and therefore I shall not speak at any length. I must say I do not claim to have the knowledge of staff principles and military organization, strategy and tactics evidenced by the previous speaker, and therefore I shall not presume to advise the minister and his advisers as to the necessary military organization for this country.
From what I have heard and observed I think the Minister of National Defence in a quiet and efficient way is doing all that is considered necessary according to the best advice he receives. The impression I get throughout the country is that the Minister of National Defence is recognized as one who does not do things with fanfare and trumpets, but is quietly working in a more efficient way than possibly a great part of the public is aware of.
I rise at this time to ask a question which I asked the minister last year. I and several other members of the house observed a military force marching past the parliament buildings some 2,000 strong. One section was bearing the latest model of Lee-Enfield rifles, while other sections showed crowns and stars on the shoulder-straps of the men. They were in full uniform. I asked the minister at that time if those troops came under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence and his reply was that they did not. I then asked the minister if it was legal to uniform, drill and equip troops -with arms, and he said that that matter would receive his consideration and was being considered by the judge advocate general. He told me that he would give me an answer at a later date.
I have not received that answer, and I rise this afternoon to ask the minister if in the period of twelve months he has finally been able to evolve an answer.

Mr. Chairman, if the minister is not answering the hon. member for Kootenay West at the moment I should like to place two questions before the minister. The first is this: Is the minister prepared to recommend that there be set up a committee on defence matters? This has been recommended ever since 1945, and on each occasion we have had the support of all opposition parties, and in fact the support of the Prime Minister on one or two occasions.
I would point out to the minister how important it is to have a group of members of this house who understand the nature of our defence problems and the steps that are being taken to meet them. Under our present set-up, we have these estimates up for discussion for the first time within two or three days of prorogation and hon. members have no opportunity to go into the question thoroughly. Yet this work of defending Canada is of vital importance to the nation. The minister of external affairs and the Minister of National Defence have emphasized the seriousness of the international situation, and the minister went so far today as to name countries.
It is vital that there should be a group of members in this house who are informed on questions of defence. We are attempting to fill up our ranks through a system of voluntary recruiting. This means that right across the country there should be people who know the facts and can urge our young men to join the forces. If we had a committee on defence matters there would be a group of members in a position to take a lead in assisting with recruiting. Two or three years ago we set up a committee on external affairs, and the fact that that committee was set up has greaty increased the interest taken in this house in matters having to do with external affairs.
My second question is this: Why do we not have a mobile brigade up to full strength? That plan was announced by the previous minister of national defence on October 16, 1945. At that time the then minister, after referring to the reserve army, went on to deal with the active army in these words:
The second will be the permanently employed active force, whose duty it will be to assist in the training and administration of the reserve army and to supply the necessary staffs, services and scientific research and development personnel, augmented by a small formation of essential field units. This formation will be maintained as a trained field force, fully equipped, ready to meet -whatever commitments may arise. Until we know more about our international obligations and consequent requirements, these active force units will be retained as a minimum and would be subject to whatever expansion
Supply-National Dejence

might later be required in the light of any obligations which we might accept to assist in maintaining the peace of the world. Preliminary estimates indicate that the numbers involved in the active permanently employed force will be between 20,000 and 25,000 all ranks.
Of course that is much higher than the number we now have. The minister pointed1 out today that the main duties of the army were, first, to prepare a force to defend Canada against sudden or direct attack now or in the near future. He went on to say that this brigade group was to be a trained and equipped force to deal with any diversionary attack. I think we are all agreed that this is the minimum of the force we should have. I cannot understand why we do not bring this brigade up to full strength and keep it at all times ready to fight. I should like to know why it is that we have deviated from the original intention, which was that this brigade group should be up to strength, fully trained and ready to fight on short notice.

May I have a word before we rise? I should like to express my appreciation to the hon. member for Nanaimo and to others who have been good enough to make kindly references to my recovery from a recent operation. As hon. members know, I am blessed with unusually good health, and therefore any interruption of it is upsetting, but I am very glad to be back in the house.
I should like also to express appreciation of the constructive and helpful way in which the debate has proceeded. A number of points have been raised to which I should like to refer, and I shall do that at the earliest possible moment when the committee next sits, which will be at eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, before the committee rose at six o'clock, some questions were raised to which I should make reply. The hon. member for Nanaimo, in his interesting remarks, referred to a matter also referred to by the hon. member for Kamloops, with regard to the readiness of the armed forces of Canada to meet sudden attack, which was the first point I made as one of the objectives of the defence forces of Canada.
When this question is raised, it is desirable to examine, however briefly, from what sources there could come a possible attack. As I said in my opening remarks, the only possible

aggressor is the Soviet union, and the only way the Soviet union can attack Canada is by sea or by air. By sea, since the Soviet union has no large fleet, attack would be possible only by submarine. Of the two, I think we may regard air as the more likely means of attack.
Without going into this in any detail, I would ask hon. members to consider the probabilities of any such attack in view of the distance, the strategic objectives that might be achieved, and the air lift the Soviet union might have.

Would the minister permit one question in order that he might deal with it in his reply? Would he concede the fact that the sea distance between Soviet Russia and the outer islands of Alaska is less than fifty miles and conceivably an attack might come that way, a short sea attack, followed by a land attack?

If such an attack occurred it would surely be made on the territory nearest to the Soviet union, that is the territory of the United States in Alaska. How they could bypass that and attack the coast of British Columbia is rather difficult to see. Should such an attack occur, the only possibility that need be considered at the present time is that of an attack by air, and there we would have to estimate the ability of the Soviet union to give an air lift that would enable such an attack to be made, and then see what would be likely to be the result of that attack.
It is difficult to say how many four-engine planes the Soviet union has, but I am sure my hon. friends are thinking of something in the neighbourhood of a division.
No, much more.

I see. Well, let us take a division. A division would probably take
1.000	four-engine planes one way, and I should think the result of that would be that the planes would be lost and that the people who landed would be lost too.
Has the minister not contemplated the possibility of a shuttle service?
A shuttle service over a distance of something like 4,000 miles is inconceivable. The attackers could be mopped up stage by stage as they come along.
What about the twenty-mile barrier to Alaska?

That is another problem, the problem of the United States of America. We are talking about Canada at the present time.

Supply-National Defence
I imagine that tfhe United States forces are adequate to deal with that. If they are not, the Americans will see to it. But when you consider the prospects of such an attack on Canada, you have to consider the possible strategic benefits which might result from an attack of that kind. The only result would be that the Soviet union would lose the
1.000	planes they had sent over, if they had
1.000	planes of that type to send over, which I doubt, and then they would lose the men they had landed.
That is why I made the point I did on the advice that was available to me, that the only kind of attack which is envisaged as possible should war break out in the immediate future is an attack of a diversionary nature which would be cleared up quite speedily.

Before the minister leaves that point, would he permit a question? I see the possibility of the loss of these 1,000 planes, provided that we have something whereby to inflict those casualties upon the enemy. I should like to know what we have in our air force at the present time, or in any other air force, which might reasonably be expected to inflict 1,000 casualties on planes coming here, if that were the case. And I presume those 1,000 planes would be at least-escorted by protective aircraft, fighters of some sort. I cannot believe that they would just crash for the fun of it.

There are no fighters in the world that can go 4,000 miles or anything like the distance that would be involved. I do not even suggest -that the planes would be knocked down as they came, because everyone knows that one, two, three or any considerable number of planes can get through in any area of the world. But the question is what happens after they do get through. I suggest that the probability that has to be taken into account in our calculations of any such attack is so slight at the present time that it is something that hardly needs being counted in the realm of active possibility; for, as I suggested, the outcome would be certain and the strategic advantages would be nil.
Why?

Why would the strategic advantage be nil?
Because the forces would be destroyed within a short time.
By whom?
By our Canadians.
By our 25,000 men?

Then my hon. friend spoke about the number of officers and men in the reserve army who were at camp during the season 1947-48. As he knows, the purpose of the reserve army camps in 1947-48 was to give training to officers, N.CD.'s and a small cadre of tradesmen. The numbers which he referred to-which were small, of course- were the numbers of officers, N.C.O.'s and tradesmen who were available to take that training at that time. In this connection and also in connection with the reference made by the hon. member for Kamloops to the article by Mr. Wallace Goforth on the nature of our reserves, I might suggest that the remarks which have been made about our reserves might have been made with equal truth about any of the reserves, let us say, the national guard in the United States or the territorial army of the United Kingdom. To indicate as clearly as I can the state of preparation arrived at in Canada in comparison with that in other countries, I should like to refer to the remarks of Lord Nathan, the government leader in the House of Lords, in a speech he made in a debate on defence on March 17, 1948, in which he said:
The forces are still in the throes of the extensive reorganization which is inevitable at the end of a great war.
When were these remarks made?

On March 17, 1948. To
