In the United States the national guard, which is the equivalent of our reserve forces, has a present strength, for the army and air force together, of 234,000. Australia and New Zealand will begin recruiting for the reserve force on July 1, 1948. I suggest to hon. members that against this background the record of achievement of our reserve forces since the war has been good. It is not as good as I should like to see it, but it reflects great credit on the officers and men who have been giving their time to this important work. When we compare the present situation with the situation as it was after the first great war, when I myself was in the non-permanent active militia, we can see a great change in the size, equipment, training facilities, pay, strength and quality of the reserve forces. Our hope is that, with the support of hon. members and others, the reserves may be built up just as speedily as possible, so that they will be an effective fighting force to take their part in the defence of Canada and serve as the nucleus of a larger force should it be necessary.
The hon. member for Nanaimo remarked on the fact that we had no submarines. That is quite true. We have never felt it necessary in Canada to have submarines, except for the purpose of anti-submarine warfare training. We feel that it is much easier for us to borrow or obtain the services of a British or a United1 States submarine when that is desirable, rather than to go into this business ourselves and try to establish a submarine service which inevitably would be dependent on either British or United States sources for the submarines and also for the modifications necessary to bring them up to date.
The hon. member for Nanaimo made an agreeable reference to the ordnance corps depot here. He remarked on the fact that, while certain men were piling puttees, different men were needed to pile bandages. That is an easy reference, if I may say so, and I interjected, "Can we use the same personnel to mix paint as we use to mix medicine?" At the depot here we have the central medical stores for all three services of Canada under the command of an officer of the Canadian army medical corps. He is in charge of the medical stores there and of their care and distribution, and also a large quantity of drugs is manufactured and quantities of supplies are made up. This work requires specially trained personnel. However, the close working relationship with .the members of the Canadian ordnance corps is indicated by the hon. member's own remark, that when he came into the part of the building that was devoted to the central medical stores, he was shown over the
[Mr Claxton.]
place by a medical officer. I do not know who else should have shown him over it.
The hon. member also referred to the question of civil defence. We have had this matter under consideration for some time; and, as hon. members know, it is a matter to which the greatest attention must be devoted to secure, first of all, close co-operation between the federal government agencies that may be concerned, which would include national defence, justice-namely, the R.C.M.P.- national health and welfare, and transport. From there we move into the field of close working relationships with the provinces and, through them, with their agencies, the municipalities. That work is in hand; preliminary studies have been made. I can assure hon. members that it is not proposed at present to set up civil defence establishments across Canada, as we believe this would be a waste of effort and time. The work will be directed to seeing what should be done, and to arrive at sound plans that can be put into effect with people with whom they have been discussed and worked out so that, in case of need, anything necessary may be done in good time. In this regard, United States secretary of defence Forrestal last May announced the appointment of a similar agency; and we shall get into touch with the people there who are actively engaged in this work as well as the people in England, and correlate their experience with our own during the last war. Then we will -work out a plan which will be constantly kept up to date as part of the war book, in preparation for any emergency.
The hon. member referred to shortages of equipment and shortage of the means of producing air force equipment. This was also referred to by the hon. member for Trinity and the hon. member for Kamloops.
Mr. SKEY,: I did not refer to any shortages. I said we should produce the equipment.

That is right. On the question of shortages referred to at some length by the hon. member for Kamloops and mentioned in passing by the hon. member for Nanaimo, I should like to know what equipment we are short of, which we should have, and which it would be useful for us to have at the present time. As far as I know, we are not short of any such equipment. We had large stocks of the latest equipment at the end of the second world war, and, in addition, since that time we have acquired considerable quantities of equipment of various types. I repeat,
I should like to know what equipment we are short of for the active or reserve forces. If we are short of any equipment which we should have we shall be glad to look into the question and see whether it would be useful for us to

Supply-National Defence
acquire that equipment now rather than run such risks as there may be-and there may be risks which we may have to run-in waiting until, in the not too distant future, we may have or be able to obtain something much better. I point out that if we follow every type of equipment we have, or that any nation which might fight in a future war has or might have, through every modification it will take a great deal more money than this country will be willing to spend on defence. The fact is that we have to make our estimate of the risks involved, and keep up to date with knowledge, information, plans and designs, and from time to time make modifications or introduce such new equipment as we feel may be justified by the need.
The hon. member for Trinity referred to the question of standardization, and one of the points he made was that the matters listed in my statement were in the wrong order, that I should have put the last thing first. I am quite willing to put it first. I assure him that his interesting and useful remarks are along the line of the discussions that have been entered into by the officers of the department from time to time with their opposite numbers in the United Kingdom and the United States; and they are the subject of constant consideration.
There was one point, however, on which I should make one comment. The hon. member did say he thought it would be a good thing if we could produce in Canada some of the planes we have to acquire either from Britain or from the United States, the Vampires from Britain and the Mustangs from the United States; and he suggested that it might be possible to have a British firm come to Canada to manufacture Vampire planes here.
That is an interesting suggestion, but I wonder what would be the implications. If such a firm came to Canada it would have a market here to the extent of such Vampire planes as we were ready to buy. They would be very expensive, because the Canadian producer would have to tool up and produce a limited number of such planes, since our needs are not large. If the planes were produced for sale in sterling bloc areas, then the British government or the purchasers would have to find Canadian dollars with which to buy the product of their subsidiary in Canada. That is not an attractive proposition, and I doubt very much whether any British firm would enter into such an undertaking. With regard to the production in Canada of American type planes, there again it would be much more economic for us to purchase the planes from the United States.
But what about the loss of exchange, and the loss of employment?

My hon. friend himself said that, even if the planes were produced in Canada, some sixty per cent of the content-I think that was the figure he indicated -would have to be purchased in the United States.
At least we would break even.
That would still leave the out-go to the United States as a considerable item.
If the minister will permit, I suggested that we produce machines here for sale to the United States as well as for use by the Canadian air force.
It is an interesting proposition which we are exploring in every direction, I can assure the hon. member-but not with Mustangs-*
I would not think so.

-because that would not be profitable. Also the Mustang is an intermediate plane which will soon be replaced by something else. No; our attitude toward this matter is that the right course for us to follow is to produce in Canada a plane designed particularly to meet Canadian needs. Toward that end we have been working for several years. Through A. V. Roe in Toronto we have produced in the Chinook engine the prototype of what looks likely to be a very good jet engine. The airframe is being tested; and if that two-seated long-range fighter tests out satisfactorily, that will be the kind of plane which we should produce in Canada. But until we can find out whether we have or have not a good plane, it would probably be wise on our part to postpone all possible purchases or ventures in this field'; not to the point of danger, but postpone it to the point where we may be able to get a Canadian plane at about the same time as we might get a plane of British manufacture. If we placed orders for Vampires or other British planes now it would be a considerable number of months before they were delivered.
I can tell the hon. member that the subject is being thoroughly explored and followed up.
The hon. member for Kamloops referred to the question of equipment as if we were short of modern equipment or modern plans. We have quantities of the latest equipment in use at the end-not the beginning-of the second world war. Our officers are in communication with their opposite numbers both in the United States and in the United Kingdom, not only revising plans but examining designs of equip-

meat, and generally keeping their fingers upon the latest developments.
The hon. member suggested that my phrase that the Canadian forces "could by themselves never deter the Russians" was ill-advised. I shall stand by my phrase. I think that is common sense. No nation of 12,000,000 people could alone deter a powerful nation, one apparently with the aggressive inclinations, and having the resources and the strength of Russia.
I, too, will stand by that statement so far as our present forces are concerned.

Yes. Then the hon. member made some reference to the air force. I made perfectly clear the reason why the air force auxiliary was not as large as we would like to see it, namely, a shortage of ground-crew. The reason why we are short of ground-crew is that there is full employment in industry, and it is difficult either to recruit trained tradesmen as regular air force personnel or to get men to join the auxiliary force and to do at night, part time, the same kind of work they are doing in the daytime. However, recently much better progress is being made, and techniques of recruiting have been developed which we hope will cure that situation.
The hon. member referred to Mr. Goforth's article, and particularly his references to the desirability of there being officers and men from the French-speaking section of the population. With that, of course, I agree. With regard to the first six points of Mr. Goforth's article, I suggest that he might have made them with equal accuracy respecting the United States, the United Kingdom or any other country, as he did respecting this country.
Oh, no.

Oh, yes. But the matter of the French-speaking personnel is a special Canadian question, and is one which I must say I have had under my own personal consideration ever since I was appointed to the department. It involves difficulties, and we are doing everything possible to meet those difficulties. May I add that we are trying to have the largest possible number of Englishspeaking officers in the armed forces learn the French language. At every headquarters throughout Canada there are voluntary classes, one of which was at national defence headquarters here in Ottawa. I believe at one time there were 276 officers taking lessons in French. We regard that as desirable, and hope that Canada will have, as nearly as possible, a bilingual army. What Mr. Goforth stated with respect to senior officers might be technically correct; but there is an associate deputy minis-

ter holding the rank of deputy minister, who is French-speaking. I refer to Colonel Matthieu, a gentleman with a distinguished war record. Two of the area commanders, Brigadier Bernatchez at Winnipeg and Brigadier Allard at Quebec, both with fine war records, are French-speaking.
The hon. member tried to make some play on my reference to the Swiss reserves. The point of my remark was to show how much more complicated the process of defence had become as compared with what it was when that kind of reserve force obtained in Switzerland. Our own reserve force units are equipped with tanks, radar apparatus, anti-aircraft guns and all the latest equipment to a point where some of them are being almost crowded out of their armouries because they have so much equipment. That is one of the points we shall have to follow up, in an endeavour to provide more accommodation.
The hon. member referred to the fact that back in March I had said that "good progress" is being made with regard to recruiting. That was an encouraging and proper kind of remark to make. I also wish to see better progress made with regard to recruiting. But the fact that in one year we have recruited a number of men roughly equivalent to the total strength of the permanent force, on the average, between 1930 and 1939, particularly at a time of full employment, is an indication that the armed forces have an appeal for the young men of this country. We hope the armed forces will continue to have that appeal, and that more of our young men will enlist.
The hon. member for Kootenay West referred to a question he raised on July 9 last with regard to the drilling of some uniformed personnel who were not members of the armed forces and who had, as he said, the latest model of Lee-Enfield rifles. At that time, following his question, I thought I had given him all the information available on the subject. A full investigation was made, but by the time he brought the matter up it was not possible to find out the full particulars. Under section 99 of the criminal code the governor in council may issue an order prohibiting drilling in uniform. I believe such an order was issued back in 1916, and since then it has been rather difficult to trace what has happened. We are not aware of any unauthorized body of men in Canada being equipped with Lee-Enfield rifles. There is a report that some Ross rifles were disposed of as surplus immediately after the first great war to some organization, and it is possible that is what his question relates to. If I have not answered him sufficiently I will try to get further information and answer him privately later.

The hon. member for Vancouver South again raised the question as to whether the government would entertain the possibility of having a committee on defence matters. As I pointed out when that question was raised last year, my own personal inclination would be in favour of that course. I can see quite a few advantages from my own point of view as minister in having an opportunity of talking things over and having them explained in such a committee. I must say, however, that the suggestion raises considerations far greater than any such personal inclinations, and those considerations I have put before the house and this committee on a previous occasion. I do not do so in any final sense, but I must say this, that once you get into the appointment of functional committees dealing with the work and operations of a single department of the government, you begin to approximate our system of government much more closely to that of the United States.
What about the committee on external affairs?

I am not going to defend the appointment of that committee, and I do not suggest that it should necessarily form a precedent for others, but I do suggest that our system of government, with the executive responsible through parliament to the people and modeled on the British system, is something we ought to cherish and to watch most carefully. The appointment of functional committees of the type suggested tends to approximate our system much more closely to that of the United States and therefore should be watched with a careful eye. However, once again I can assure the hon. member for Vancouver South that his suggestion has a lot to commend it, and I shall be very glad indeed to call it to the attention of my colleagues. But there again the appointment of committees is a matter for the judgment of the house and it is for the house to decide.
The other question the hon. member asked was with regard to the mobile brigade. That mobile brigade still forms, as I indicated in my statement today, the main agency by which Canada would deal with any direct attack on Canada. There has been no abandonment of it whatever. It is in training now. The armoured and infantry battalions have been grouped together at Petawaiwa for the first time and this summer will engage in unit training. The other branches of it are at Rivers, where the army-air co-operation school is located, at Chilliwack where there is the engineers' school, and at Shilo the artillery school, and other branches are at other places.
The brigade is being trained. We have got through the stage of training the trainers, which is the first stage, and now the men themselves are receiving unit training.
My question was, why is the force not recruited up to full strength?
It is being recruited, as fast as the recruits come in, toward full strength. I hope I have answered the questions raised, and if there are any others I rfiall be glad to answer them.

Mr. Chairman, we appreciate the 'minister's returning tonight to give answers to the various questions which were raised here this afternoon, because I understand that he is really breaking doctor's orders in being here, that he is, in military language, A.W.O.L. from hospital. There are various other questions I should like to raise and I believe other members have questions but perhaps we can raise them on other items. No doubt an opportunity will be given when these estimates are before us again.
There is just one thing I should like to say before the minister goes, and that is to point out what seems somewhat of an inconsistency between the statement that he read and the remarks that he has made this evening. This afternoon he referred to the fact that it was now possible to set down Canada's present defence aims and objectives. They are (1) To provide a force estimated to be necessary to defend Canada against any sudden direct attack that could be or is likely to be directed against her in the near future. When we pointed out the fact, as we gathered it from other parts of his statement, that we felt Canada had not anything in the way of a defence force to meet this attack, the minister this evening said:	Oh, there is not going to
be any such threat. That is like putting up a coconut-shy just for the purpose of throwing balls at a coconut.

I hate to get into this discussion with military experts. The only practical suggestion made this afternoon and this evening was that made by the hon. member for Vancouver South when he suggested, as he has done on previous occasions, that a committee of this house be set up for the purpose of studying the defences of Canada in co-operation with the military authorities. Over 100 members of this house are ex-service personnel with war experience in varying capacities, and they could contribute something to the headquarters personnel in mapping out the defence requirements and defence
Supply-National Defence

estimates of the country. I would strongly urge the minister to give that suggestion his serious consideration.
But what really prompted me to get up at this time was the repeated emphasis by hon. members to my right that the defence plans of Canada must be based on a threat of aggression from Russia. I think that is absolutely wrong.
The minister said it.
I think it is absolutely wrong for any member of this house representing the public of Canada to take the attitude that the defence of Canada must be built on the possibility of aggression by Russia.
Our whole point was that it should 'be built against aggression from any point, including Russia.
That is not what you said.
I know what I said. You were not here when I said it.
I remember when you made your first speech and your second speech. I listened carefully-
It shows how wrong you were.
Just a minute; wait until I am through.
Not a man overseas.

I am going to tell you something about your own part of the country with regard to defence which I think is essential at this time, and I hope you will be doing something about it before I am through. Defence, as everything else, is a practical matter. It is not a matter of dreaming or of theories. It is only about three years since we finished a war, a war to end wars, a war against aggression and tyranny, and we broke the only force in the world that threatened the world. All the nations which are united today in the united nations were allied together for that purpose. We succeeded in a common objective, namely, defeating the forces of aggression. Since the end of that war we formed the united nations. That is the cornerstone of Canada's foreign policy, and also the cornerstone of Canada's defence policy.
It is more like a millstone.

All right; when we accepted the charter of the united nations we decided to band ourselves together for the purpose of bringing the nations together in one world, of setting up a common front of the nations of the world, which were allied together, to save
CMr. Gillis.]
democracy and freedom and to expand it. We formed ourselves in what, in my opinion, is the basis of government at the international level. There are quarrels, and all that kind of thing, but under the united nations charter Canada and all the nations which are within that machinery today, decided that certain things were to be done to secure the peace of the world.
An international peace force was to be set up. We had a common objective; we said we would crack down on aggressors, and Russia as part of the international machine-
She is the brakes.

Just a minute, now. She may or may not be. Do not forget this. It is not as simple as all that. You are dealing with people of different nationalities, different languages, different outlooks on life, different experiences, backgrounds and environments. Perhaps her thinking is conditioned on her experiences, her background and her environment. I am very hopeful. I am not prepared to stand up in my place in this house at any time and advocate, or listen to someone advocate, that the basic policy on defence in Canada should be built up on the fear of aggression from one of our former allies. I do not think it exists. I am not afraid of a major war from any direction in your lifetime or in mine.
What my hon. friends fail to realize is that the war which they fear has been going on since 1945. It is an economic war.
All we are afraid of is that, after fighting a war from 1939 to 1945, we may have to do so again. We do not want to have to do so again.
We are not going to have to fight another war unless you promote it.

What are you advocating
-disarmament ?
No. If you listen for a minute I shall tell you.

Give in to the commies and you will not have to fight another war.
I am not giving in to the commies at all, and my hon. friend has too much sense not to know that.
You are not realistic.

I am trying to be realistic. This standing up in the house and saying we are afraid that someone is going to attack us just will not do. I am telling you I am not afraid that someone is going to attack us.

That is fine.
You are being swallowed up every day, and you do not realize it. There is an economic war going on.
Speak for yourself.
Russia has been kidding you that she is going to shoot you some day. In the meantime you are putting the clothes over your head in bed at night and are afraid that the bogey man will get you.
Is that the way Czechoslovakia was kidded?
Certainly it is.
Is that what the Minister of Defence thinks?

I am not worrying about what the Minister of Defence thinks. He has no more responsibility for this than you have. Little countiy after little country has been absorbed while you sat down and urged the Minister of Defence to build more and bigger planes, bigger tanks and bigger something else.
Nonsense.
While the other fellow came along and took you over; that is all.
Certainly if you were here he would.

There is going to be no shooting war. You do not need to worry about that. There is an economic war on now. The faster you fellows get that through your heads, the better it will be for Canada and for the world.
Certainly if we go on as the hon. member suggests we would have a shooting war.

If you would only get down to realities and talk common sense.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

Some hon. members never seem to learn much in this house. I think the minister is being realistic. He has brought forward a pretty reasonable program of defence for Canada. He is not preparing for war. He has not told anyone in the house so far that he is afraid of an attack from Russia or from the United States. If we are to learn something about national defence I think the only
sensible proposal that has been put forward in the house was put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver South. Let us appoint the hon. member for Kamloops, the hon. member for Trinity and the hon. member for Vaneouver-Burrard, who is so much interested in national defence and in arming against the aggression from an imaginary enemy that does not exist, on a board with officials of national defence, and let them have a look at things as they really are, things that cannot be brought up in this house. I am reasonably sure that if that were done it would convince them that the thing that has to be done in the future to prevent war-
Czechoslovakia was not taken over?
She was taken over because of stupid people-
Like yourself.

-who hung on to something that did not exist in life. They created a form of thinking along the lines of that which hon. members are thinking tonight, and the other fellow walked in, in the meantime, and took things over while you were asleep.
My friend, you are asleep.
Took it over with machine guns.

No, there was no shooting. He just took it over from the Tories who were asleep. They went sound asleep with the clothes over their heads worrying about an attack from an imaginary enemy, and in the meantime the enemy walked in and took them over.
Just as you are doing in this country.
We are not doing so badly on this matter of defence.
Just the way you are doing in this country.

I think we are being fairly sensible about it. I think the government of Canada and the sensible people of the North American continent realize that the thing that will offset war in the future is living up to the charter of the united nations, feeding hungry people, raising their standards, eliminating insecurities and fears that drag half the world down into the ashpit. That is what will avoid war in the future; not building up armies and preaching wars against a people who a short time ago were very respectable in this house as our allies.

There is one thing of a practical nature I should like to say to the minister. He mentioned tonight that in the field of jet aircraft he was carrying on an extensive development at the A. V. Roe company in Toronto. I know this does not come within his jurisdiction, but I point out to him that on Sunday-this is -Jiiursday-a strike vote is to be taken in that -plant. The government has considerable jurisdiction over" that plant. There is apt to be an interruption on that aeroplane in which the minister is so much interested. I am suggesting that he get in touch with the Minister of Labour and try to offset any labour difficulties there, so that we may get the necessary planes to offset the inevitable war that my hon. friends to the right are talking so much about.

The subject which was before the committee, as I understood, was the defence of Canada, but the hon. member who has last spoken has sought to supplant it with another issue altogether. With him I would be glad to enter into controversy at any moment, because his ideas are so erroneous that they really should be answered. He has spoken about the economic war, which of course has no relation to the question of national defence. He has spoken about people being asleep in this country. Perhaps we were asleep in this country until what went on in Czechoslovakia and other countries woke us up. If we were not wakened up, as perhaps we were not by what took place from 1935 to 1939, and between 1939 and 1945, I hope we have been wakened up by what took place in 1948 in Czechoslovakia, where, under the guise of so-called economic war, which was fostered by those who wanted Russia to take over their country, we saw Russia step in and take that country without a shot being fired, as the hon. member says. However, that situation does not prevail in Canada. There is opportunity for all in Canada, and the only people who are concerned to go around and say a situation exists in Canada which justifies Russia or anyone else taking us over are my hon. friends to the left.
That is not true.
I know it is true.
Stick to national defence.

The hon. member for Cape Breton South says, "Stick to national defence". I was sticking to national defence until he introduced this extraneous issue. I wish, as does the hon. member for Nanaimo, and every other member of this house, to see the Minister of National Defence released for the moment from his responsibility; and, had it not been for what the hon. member for Cape Breton South

said, which was so erroneous that it required some answer, I would not have spoken at the moment. But the fact is that those who were alseep from 1935 to 1939 and those who, like my hon. friends, have been asleep from 1939 to 1948, are asleep no longer. We know the issues. We know that this economic war they talk about is just phony as far as Canada is concerned, and we are not going to allow ourselves to become the prey to any phony economic war or any actual war of aggression with armed forces. That is why we have been discussing the defence of Canada, and that is why we have been criticizing the policy of the Minister of National Defence.
With respect to the minister, I have this to say. Imperfect as I think his policy is, it is so much nearer perfection, so much more realistic and so much more attuned to the best interests of Canada than the sort of nonsense talked by my hon. friends to the left tonight that I will say no more about it at the moment, but reserve my right to discuss it at a later day.
Item agreed to.

In view of the remarks made by the hon. member for Yorkton this morning, and in view of the remarks made by the minister regarding the report of the committee on Indian affairs, I consider it essential that I should say something about that question at this time, since I was a member of the committee from the time of its inception in 1946.
Since 1867 there have been only two parliamentary inquiries into Indian affairs. One took place in 1920 and another in 1926; and, since that time, until 1946, a period of twenty years, no attempt has been made to rectify the injustices that exist in the present act.
I am not blaming the officials of the department, because I believe that most of them are sincere and conscientious in their efforts under the existing legislation. They do the best they can, as evidenced by the co-operation given to us during the sittings of the committee that considered the Indian Act. In that committee, after listening to all the delegations and studying the briefs presented, we tried to recommend amendments to the act which we felt would be accepted by the majority of the Indians of Canada.

I tried to be fair this morning. I did not wish to make any remarks under the estimates of this branch; I wanted to defer them until concurrence in the report was moved. I gave the minister a chance to assure us that concurrence in the report of the Indian affairs committee would be moved, but that was not forthcoming, and I can only say that it is now obvious that concurrence will not be moved.
It is incredible that after three sessions, with this committee sitting and this house considering Indian affairs, this report is not to be concurred in before the end of the session. It simply means that the work of the committee has been a failure, if this parliament will not adopt that report before the end of the session. The work of the committee has been useless.
Representing the largest and, I might add, the most advanced Indian reserve in Canada,
I say on their behalf that I disagree with the general idea advanced in most of the sittings of the committee that there should be complete assimilation of the Indian population.
I most heartily disagree with that. The Indians of the Six Nations tribe are a very proud people. They do not wish to be completely assimilated, thereby losing their identity as Indians. The Indians of the Six Nations reserve have proven their ability to govern themselves. They have set an example that could well be followed today throughout the world, in the fact that six tribes which were at war at one time were able to settle their differences and are now, as they have been for many years, living in complete harmony with one another.
It would seem almost futile to discuss this report at the present moment, because if a motion for concurrence is not forthcoming, then the whole thing will be thrown out.
As I said before, it seems to me a most ridiculous situation, after this committee has sat for three sessions and has done the amount of work it has done, that this report should not be brought forth and concurred in.
I wish to say just a few words with regard to a couple of the recommendations in this report. The first is No. 8 and is headed "Social and economic status of Indians and their advancement." I will just read it:
Your committee recommends that the govern ment consider the advisability of granting a pension to aged, blind, or infirm Indians. This is in addition to recommendations previously made with regard to the social and economic advancement of Indians.
I was greatly disappointed to note that the committee thought they hadi to recommend that the government consider the advisability of this sort of thing. It should have passed
that stage many years ago. It should recommend that these aged Indians be considered the same as any other people in this country and be given the old age pension.
The committee recommended that the Indians should have the vote on the status of urban dwellers. That recommendation, however, did not find its way to the House of Commons, through the neglect or failure of someone to see that it did. Some days ago in the house an amendment was moved to the Dominion Elections Act, and it was voted down. Why should these people not be given the vote, especially those on the Six Nations reserve at Brantford who, as I have said, are more advanced than most across the country? Why should these people not be allowed to vote? The only tax they do not pay is the land tax on their reserve. They pay the other taxes, such as sales, excise, and gasoline taxes, and income tax on money earned off the reserve. Therefore I think it is time these people were given representation.
Since coming here and acting as a member of the Indian Act committee, I have always taken the stand that Indians of ability should be given positions in the branch, and I still stick to that stand. I am glad to see the recommendation made that the assistant deputy, or commissioner, should be a Canadian of Indian descent.
In conclusion, I urge the government to see that the motion for concurrence in this report is made before the end of the session; because, if that is not done, the committee might just as well not have met these past three sessions.

Item agreed to.
Immigration branch-
228. For expenditures in connection with looking after Canadian interests abroad, $100,000.

I do not know whether I am in order, but I want to urge on the minister that he do something to increase his staff overseas, so that the technicalities in connection with immigrants may be overcome more quickly. I know the staffs over there are short-handed. We want all the good immigrants we can get in this country. If we do not make it a little bit easier and make it possible to get over the .technicalities more quickly, we shall lose out in this matter. I urge the minister to do something along the line I have suggested.

I have in my hand an editorial from the Telegraph-Journal of Saint John, dated June 16, 1948. I do not propose to read it all; in fact, I do not know whether I would be in order if I did so. But I should
Supply-Mines and Resources

like to draw it to the attention of the minister. It is headed "Intelligence not wanted", and it goes on to say:
Ten Baltic and Polish young women who have just disembarked in Canada, after a trip from displaced persons' camps in Germany, make the bitter complaint that this country seems to put a premium on stupidity. To get here, they claim, they had to hide the fact that one girl studied commerce for two years in Riga, another was a student nurse in a hospital, another a clerk, another a pharmacy worker. They were quietly advised by their friends to appear "good and dumb"-and so they were allowed to come to Canada. Meanwhile, Australia is gladly taking girls with brains as well as brawn.
The editorial goes on and points out:
. . . those who_ are doing the selecting in Europe have been trying to pick out girls who will not use maid's work as merely a subterfuge to- get into Canada and then try immediately to quit their jobs and seek "white collar" work.
That may be the object the immigration authorities have in view in selecting these girls. Then the editorial goes on to say:
But it would be interesting, just the same, to know what work Australia is able to offer to intelligent and educated D.P. girls that Canada too, can't offer.
Does the minister care to make any comment on that editorial or to throw some light or. what happened? If that is correct, why is it that girls with some education and some intelligence are not allowed in the country, or apparently they have to play dumb to get in here?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext:
I am quite sure the hon. member for St. Johm-Albert is not taking that editorial or that newspaper story at its face value. We in Canada have ten girls for every one that has gone to Australia, I am informed. They are girls of intelligence. They are girls who are, for the time being, at least, doing domestic work in Canada and working in institutions. We are encouraging people of intelligence; that is the type of people we want here in Canada. The reporter in this particular case-and I have read the editorial.
I believe it is, or the newspaper article-must have got hold of the odd crank there always is in any movement of immigration.
Is any intelligence test required before these girls are admitted?
There is a general screening, I may say; and some of our rejections are on the basis of lack of intelligence.

Can the minister give an answer to the question if it is put in this way? In selecting girls for admission to Canada, if a girl said that her occupation was secretarial 
work, typist, schoolteacher, or something of that kind, would she have the same chance of getting in as a girl who said her work was domestic service?
She would have a better chance to come to Canada if she could convince us that she intended to work as a domestic or in an institution, temporarily.
Then that would mean that the girl who would not work as a domestic would have a poorer chance of getting into Canada?
I think that is quite right.

Then I imagine the point made by the editorial is correct, that in selecting persons to come to Canada we do not want educated women who will not work in domestic service. We want girls who are not so well educated, who cannot fill jobs which require a certain amount of education or training.
That is not quite fair or quite correct.
Then will the minister please explain it?

We are desirous of getting intelligent girls to come to Canada in this immigration movement, but girls who for a term are willing to do domestic work or work in institutions. There are plenty of intelligent prospective immigrants to select from, and that is the kind we get.

We should not confuse the words "intelligence" and "education". A person with no education at all may be very intelligent, but she is limited in the services she can render. She cannot offer the same service as a person with more formal education or more specialized education. A stenographer, a schoolteacher, or a girl trained in secretarial work can do housekeeping, but a girl who has not been trained cannot do those jobs. According to the minister's answer, as I see it, the girl who has had training in office work has a poorer chance of obtaining entry into Canada than a girl who has not.

I realize that the minister has just taken over this department and that it may be difficult for him to reply to certain questions in detail. However, should he be in a position, with the assistance of his officials, to answer certain questions which I should1 like to ask, I would be grateful to him. Has the minister figures showing the percentage of the proposed immigrants from among the displaced persons who have been rejected on medical grounds.

Supply-Mines and Resources
The second question is, what are the health requirements or health standards off the department as applied to displaced persons and refugees? To put it in another way, what are the required minimum health standards which must be possessed toy displaced persons and refugees before they are admitted- to Canada?
In this connection I would point out to the minister that the officials of the preparatory commission of IRO are of opinion- that the health requirements of most countries are excessively high. Having in mind the conditions under which these people have lived for the past nine years, I consider it unreasonable of us to ex-peot them to be in perfect health. In cases I find the department usually refuses to admit displaced persons for health reasons. Then, when these persons refer the matter to me they explain that if one member of the family is just below the standard required the entire family is refused entry. At its sittings in Geneva last January, the preparatory commission of IRO felt that something should be done about this matter of the excessively high health standards required by a number -of countries. In one part of the report I find this statement:
It is the opinion of the executive secretary, that if the family unit can become self-supporting in a new country, the presence of one sick member of the family should not debar the whole family.
Then it goes on:
It is undoubtedly true that at present selection missions are removing the best of the refugees from the point of view of physical fitness, and are in themselves creating a hard core of the unfit. It is the view of the executive secretary that the standards imposed -are excessively high.
I could quote many passages fro-m- this lengthy -report, but I think -it will suffice if I refer to only one other, -which says that if the calorie intake of any section of the population falls below this emergency subsistence level- for any length of time, serious consequences must Ibe expected.
The daily calorie intake that should be provided for displaced persons is set -at 1,900. According to the report, I find that in -the French zone of Austria, fo-r instance, at times the people receive less than 1,000 calories a day, while the amount required by a normal person is about three thousand. So the minister will -realize that at this time it is not fair for us to demand that displaced -persons come up to the health standards we set prior to the second- great war.
There are so many arguments in favour of setting lowered health requirements for displaced persons that I do not think I should mention many more, but I believe the
humanitarian aspect should enter into this problem. The Canadian immigration teams and the department have been taking the attitude that they are dealing with persons as so much physical labour or so many numbers. We are not treating them as human beings; and I feel that at this time we certainly ought to take the human element into consideration.
I have before me a number of letters which I selected at random from the group of more than a thousand I now have running currently. An elderly lady finds herself in a displaced persons camp in Munich, Germany, which is in the United States zone. She is sixty-five years of age. She has been refused admits tance to Canada; yet this old lady has not a single relative anywhere in Europe. She has two sons in Windsor, Canada, and a daughter in St. Catharines. Her two sons and her daughter are willing to put up any guarantee that the department may wish to set. Yet, just because this woman is sixty-five years old and not in the best of health, she is denied the privilege of coming to Canada. She has no contagious disease of any kind, and I for one cannot see why the department could not admit this woman to Canada, so long as her sons and her daughter are prepared to take care of her.
Surely that would be a proper thing to do. Yet we treat these people as if they were not human beings. I have here another case; and I received three letters in one day from this person. He states that, because the medical examiners have found that his son's child was not in the best of health, it has been ruled that this family cannot come to Canada until and unless the child is completely cured.
Let me say to the minister that if he had an opportunity to see the conditions under which these people live he would know that the majority of them have to live in a space of about thirty-six square feet per individual. No child can become healthy under conditions of that kind. There is no hope that the child can recover, or that any other person could recover, unless they are given better quarters to live in and better food to eat.
Then I have the case of a young man on whose behalf someone has applied for entry into Canada. But, no, he was too light. His weight was not what the Canadian health officials thought it should be, with the result that he was rejected. The same man was accepted -by the United States army, and is today in the armed services of the United States. If he is heavy enough for the United States army, surely we should not have refused him admission to Canada.
Supply-Mines and Resources

And so on, down the line. I have with me a chart which has been drawn up by the preparatory commission of the international relief organization. When the medical examiners of that organization take down their records certain health standards are indicated. This chart sets forth an exacting health standard, a high standard indeed. However, even though the international relief organization approves the health standard of certain proposed immigrants, Canadian doctors refuse it. Surely, if a person is healthy enough to satisfy the doctors of IRO he should be healthy enough to satisfy our Canadian doctors; unless, of course, we want to rule out completely the humanitarian consideration, and various other considerations which enter into this matter. If we are not interested in the future of these people, and if we do not want them to be interested in the future of Canada, then that is the way to proceed. But if we want them to build up their homes in Canada; if we want them to spend their future years here; if we want them to be citizens of this country, then, even if there are one or two members in a family who may be a little weaker than the others, we should allow the weaker ones to come with the stronger ones.
The minister knows very well, coming from the same province as I do, the progress the pioneers of these various stocks have made in western Canada, and the contribution they have made to the development of our country. Surely we should have no doubt that they will be able to look after themselves, once they get here. All we have to do is to look at the relief records between 1930 and 1939. I can say with pride that we shall not find many names on those records of people of European origin. They got along as best they could, and perhaps on a little less than other people would require.
I say, therefore, that we should not require so much from them. When I take my seat I should like to have the minister comment on what I have said. I have been receiving letters every day from all parts of Europe and Canada. People are panicky because of the attitude of the Canadian medical men who examine these people, and who set up such rigid standards. It is unreasonable-and I say that frankly.
Would the minister explain to the committee the situation with respect to what is known as form 55. I have before me many letters, and I have others in my files, all of which state that sons, brothers or other relatives have remained in Europe for a long time, having failed to receive approval from the immigration authorities because form 55 has been lost. What does this mean? It was

explained to me by one of the Canadians who worked for the preparatory commission of IRO that a Canadian immigration official will call at a certain camp with the purpose of questioning a certain number of persons. The doctor will have a certain number of persons to examine medically. He may bring with him 100 files so as to examine 100 persons in that camp. However, the doctor becomes tired and decides to move on to another camp perhaps fifty or one hundred miles away. Having examined only fifty, he will not examine the other fifty, but will just leave them and take the documents along with him, moving off to the far end of Germany.
Another examiner will come to the same camp a few days later. Then, when these people ask him if they should appear for examination and questioning they receive the obvious answer, "We are sorry; we cannot deal with you because your form has been lost". Surely some system should be organized to see that only so many forms are taken by officials at a time, and that all are dealt with. Then these persons could be advised that they have to appear at a certain camp, and they would know where they stand. But this procedure of dragging the matter along month after month is not fair.
I have the case of a man here whose brother-in-law is at Bonnyville, Alberta. He states that his application was approved nearly two years ago. He has been waiting for the last six months in a transit camp, and he states that his form 55 is missing. Therefore he has to wait.
I do not like bringing up these matters. I would rather wish to be able to rise in my place and thank the government and the department for doing their best in dealing with this tragic problem-because it is a tragic problem. I appeal to the minister and to the officials of his department to do something, and to see that these things are organized on a somewhat better basis than they have been prior to now.
I know, for instance, that the Canadian immigration branch has an office in Heidelberg, Germany, in the United States zone. That is the Canadian immigration headquarters in the United States zone of Germany. These poor Canadian officials-I call them poor because they are asked to do an almost impossible task-have to take their typewriters and a large number of files along with them and drive in a car from camp to camp to examine prospective immigrants. They have no office; they simply call at a camp and are given a room where they can sit down and examine the people. They spend a little time in a camp and do not know where they are to

Supply-Mines and Resources
sleep or where they are to eat. The situation is not at all what it should be. If we are really serious about this thing, we should establish smaller stations where our officials can examine the people, so that they will not be forced to wait for months and months in a transit camp until some official comes along and examines them. The situation is bad;
I am sorry I must say that, but I feel that these unfortunate people deserve more consideration than they have been getting.
I have another question. Has the department medical examiners attached to Canadian embassies in Poland, Roumania, Hungary, *Czechoslovakia and the U.S.S.R.? If not, where should prospective immigrants residing in these countries go for their medical examination? They should be instructed exactly where to go. As it is now, they write all over creation trying to find out to whom they should apply for exit visas and permits to *come to Canada or to whatever other country they wish to go. Again, what procedure should be followed by these prospective immigrants residing in the countries I have named if settlement arrangements in Canada are found satisfactory? That procedure should be fully explained and the instructions set out clearly in the regulations, or perhaps a bulletin could be issued to the press.
I have another question which the minister is not obliged to answer. It has to do with the assistance which IRO is supposed to give to cover the transportation costs of an immigrant from a displaced persons camp. In the speech I made in this house on May 29 I quoted a paragraph from the minutes of the preparatory commission of IRO, in which it was clearly stated that, as from the middle of January- I think that was the date-even individual immigrants might apply for assistance to cover their transportation costs. That information has not been made public. I know a man in Winnipeg who is working on the railroad as an ordinary labourer and who has paid the fares of nine members of his family whom he is bringing over from Europe. Nobody had told him that part of the transportation costs may be covered and should be covered by IRO, according to the decision of the preparatory commission of IRO, by the money voted by IRO for that purpose. Surely that information should be made public. A shrewd person who knows about this assistance will take advantage of it, but those who know nothing about it pay the transportation costs themselves.
Again, any firm which brings out a group of workers is reimbursed by IRO for the transportation costs. Most industrialists know about that. As a matter of fact, I suppose
that IRO itself gets in touch with the industrialists and tells them: You paid out so much for transportation costs, and here is a cheque to cover it. But the ordinary individual does not know about this assistance, and so, I say, more light should be thrown on the various procedures that should be followed by the ordinary people, so that they will be told what they ought to know.
I cannot for the life of me understand why we treat this matter so lightly. To bring out an immigrant from a displaced persons camp to Canada is like pulling a tooth; it is so difficult. Certain cases which I referred to the department nearly three years ago are still pending. I have written and written to the department about them, and finally I get almost a stereotyped reply that the matter is now out of the department's hands and that I should apply to IRO. Then I write to IRO in Switzerland, and I get an answer from them that, so far as they are concerned, they have approved the application, and that it is out of their hands. Then I write to the Canadian immigration office in Europe and they tell me that they have approved it. The net result of all this is that the prospective immigrant is kept waiting for months and months before final action is taken.
The most unfortunate group of all in these displaced persons camps is the one composed of middle-aged and older people, fifty years of age and over. For those over sixty years of age there is absolutely no hope. After six years of war and three years in a displaced persons camp, living on the rations they have had to live on, their chances are very slim indeed unless some country will take up their case from a humanitariain standpoint. I appeal especially on behalf of these older people. If there is a relative in Canada who is willing to guarantee that his mother or father or uncle or some other relative in a displaced persons camp will not become a public charge in Canada, Canada should accept that guarantee and let the immigrant come forward.

Just before the minister answers the able remarks just made by the member for Vegreville, I should like to put in a word in support of what he said regarding form 55. These forms are filled out here; once they are approved, they go overseas, and then the merry-go-round begins. Form 55 is lost, or it is never where it is wanted. It is a terrible disappointment to Canadians in this country who want to bring members of their families to Canada to find that when they can provide for them, when they are acceptable under our laws, they still have months and months to wait, while they chase form 55 halfway around
*

Supply-Mines and Resources
Europe and finally track it down, Once they are approved and examined there, they have to wait for many -more hard months. I know of the shipping difficulties that the government have, and I have some sympathy with them on that score; but it seems to me that this administrative set-up could be a little more expeditiously handled.
I should like to endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Vegreville in that respect particularly, and a lot of other things that he said tonight to the minister.

I have listened attentively to the most distressing picture painted by the hon. member for Vegreville, and supported by the hon. member for Trinity. It is quite possible that, because the minister and the officials are sympathetic, we appreciate the distressing nature of the situation.
The department officials, and particularly Mr. Jolliffe who is in front of me, can tell a much sadder story than the one which has been recounted by the hon. member for Vegreville, because Mr. Jolliffe is a man of a large heart, patient, sympathetic, capable and1, I think, is doing a wonderful job as head of the immigration branch. I can assure hon. members that the department's approach to this problem is one of sincere sympathy.
In dealing with the various points mentioned by the hon. member for Vegreville, I shall be as brief as I can and still give what information I can. A question was asked as to the proportion of immigrants or displaced persons who have been rejected for medical reasons. It may be possible to get those figures, but I am sorry we have not them at the present time. If we can get them I shall be glad to give them to the hon. member or to any other hon. member interested.
I was asked as to the minimum health standards set up by the department. There are two tests, the tuberculosis test and the venereal disease test; otherwise people are expected to be in good mental and physical health.
They are X-rayed.

Yes, they are all
X-rayed. The comment has been made that the standards are excessively high. I question that statement, but I believe that the standards should be kept high. Certain allowances are made, when we get our medical reports that the state of an immigrant's health is directly attributable to the life he or she has lived since becoming a displaced person, so long as there are not serious health difficulties such as tuberculosis or communicable diseases.
We do not break up families. If one member is much below the standard or is

sufficiently below the standard that he or she cannot be accepted we do not accept the other members of the family. That is the policy of the department. Whether it is right or wrong it is the policy arrived at after a great deal of earnest thought.
I may say that our doctors examine the applicants for admission to Canada and our immigration authorities take the advice of these doctors. Canada has done more for displaced persons than all other non-European countries put together. We have already admitted approximately 25,000 displaced persons.
How many of these came in group movements, and how many as individuals?

Nineteen thousand
came in group movements, and about 7,000 as close relatives.
The matter of what is to be done with displaced persons who are substandard in health will have to be settled in some kind of international agreement.
In connection with form 55, the application forms are all sent to the teams in Germany by air mail as soon as the application is approved. In addition, the approved names are sent to the international relief organization by air mail. The IRO is responsible for bringing the immigrants to the immigration teams.
Have we a representative on the IRO?

A number of Canadians. The question was asked as to what procedure was taken on applications in Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and the U.S.S.R. These go to the Canadian missions where they are examined by a doctor approved by the Canadian authorities. We have no missions in Hungary or Roumania.
Comment was made on the cost of bringing these displaced persons to Canada, and reference was made to the fact that their relatives are being asked to pay for them where they are able to do so. The international relief organization has a limited budget and has to stretch it as far as possible. Canada has contributed $3,000,000 up to February of this year. That is more than anyone else has contributed except the United States of America and the United Kingdom.

Are any companies reimbursed for the cost of bringing them out, and are any private individuals reimbursed? The hon. member for Vegreville brought up that point.

Supply-Mines and Resources

That, of course is the
responsibility of IRO, not of the immigration branch. I brought it out for the purpose of clarifying the issue, so that this information would be published by the IRO or perhaps by the immigration branch, in order that the people would know who is responsible for the cost. Of course IRO is responsible.

I have answered briefly, Mr. Chairman, but I have covered the principal points raised by the hon. member for Vegreville. I want to assure the committee that this whole problem is approached with the greatest sympathy. It is an overwhelming problem. I cannot understand how some of the officials in the immigration branch have stood up under the pressure to which they are being subjected. They are doing their utmost, as I say, with a difficult problem, and they deserve a great deal of credit.

I listened with great
attention, as I am sure the committee did, to the hon. member for Vegreville. He made some points that are worthy of careful consideration by the immigration branch. One of the points that impressed me was the turning down of a whole family because one person in the family was not able to make the grade, to put it that, way, from a physical standpoint. We should look at the question somewhat differently from that of ordinary immigration. These are refugees. A refugee, if I understand the term, is a person seeking sanctuary, and when you give sanctuary to that person you are not doing so in order to benefit yourself. When we allow immigrants to come in; when we urge them to come to this country, we do so ordinarily because we want them, because it is good for us and not necessarily because it is good for them. It is purely a business proposition.
It is not altogether selfish.

There is no harm in being selfish as long as a person is intelligently selfish. The fact of the matter is that we are doing it because we want these people here. But when we are doing something for refugees wre are doing it for their benefit and not for ours, and it is hypocritical of us to take credit for the fact that we allow healthy persons from the refugee camps to come in, in order to make good producers in Canada. After every country has taken the cream-I do not know how many were there in the first place, a million and a half or so-who will take the rest? Who will take the cripples, the maimed, the ill. who cannot be productive in any country? If we are to do this in a
Christian charitable way, we Should be prepared to take our share of the sick and the afflicted, as well as those who can become good producers.

Is there any screening in the case of a parent who comes to Canada from the United Kingdom if a son living here undertakes that the parent will not become a public charge? Does the parent coming into the country have to be screened? Is he allowed to come in' if the son undertakes that he will not be a public charge?
The only screening is to safeguard health. It is purely a matter of health.

Is there any screening of the son who lives in this country, or is his financial condition gone into to find out whether he is in a position to take care of the parent to see that that parent does not become a public charge?
I am informed that in such cases exceptions have been made.

I do not wish to go into particular cases, but I wish to bring to the attention of the minister or of the head of the immigration branch a case which I shall ask him to look into, because it is one in which, in my opinion, there was not proper screening, and in which the financial position of the son, who must have undertaken to look after this parent, was not carefully investigated. I refer to people who formerly lived in this country, who had to be looked after while they were here, and who went back to the old country. Now they are in this country again and are a cause of some worry to charitable people in the neighbourhood.
Is it a fact that no record is kept of people emigrating from Canada and going to other lands? Is no record kept by the government?

I am informed that we do not keep any record of people going out from Canada.
Mr. MACDONNELL OMuskoka-Ontario): I wish to say one word by way of agreement with the the remark made by the hon. member for Vancouver East. I understand that the United States has undertaken to receive a substantial number of displaced persons, and I wish to know w'hether we have considered our duty in the matter, because if we leave the whole of the task to those who are less able than ourselves it will never be done.

With reference to the question I asked, I was informed that the dominion bureau of statistics gave information to the

senate that over 6,000,000 people had left Canada since confederation. Where did they get the record?
I am informed, from the United States figures.

speechtext: Item 224, Indian affairs branch.

With your consent, Mr. Chairman, I can go ahead. Under this item I wish to discuss fur conservation for a moment or two. I have before me the answer to that now. I want to know how much of this vote was spent on fur conservation. I am informed that the bulk of it is spent on fur conservation, but I had a request that I find out what benefit this is to the Indians. A letter was written to me a short time ago to which I tried to give a fair answer, and with the information I can get here this evening it will be a good record. One fur conservation project which the department has had under its care is known as Summerberry. It was intended to conserve muskrats and it has turned out to be of great profit to the department. When I say "great profit" I mean that it is paying its own way. I wish to put on record the fact that this year, from the Summerberry rehabilitation of musk-

rats project, 103,000 skins were sold which realized 1294,580. If the department can continue this work of fur conservation it will do a great deal to benefit the Indians.
Another question which I would ask the minister to answer is this. Of what benefit is this to the Indians, and how many Indians are employed in the trapping of these muskrats? I understand from one of the officials that one-third of the trappers each year are Indians and that they earn enough money each year to equal a monthly income throughout the whole year. The reason I asked to have this put on the record is that I want to send' it to those who have been making the inquiry; and I know it is a good thing to send out, because the department has made a wonderful success of its fur conservation proposition in Summerberry near The Pas in Manitoba and also in any conservation areas it has under its control.
The hon. member has asked what benefit this project is to the Indian. We require that one-third of the trapping licences will be reserved for Indians.

The question I wish to ask the minister has to do with item 225, $1,240,000. The item is for three different things: to defray the expenses of the interdepartmental committee on air surveys, payments to commercial companies and payments to the Royal Canadian Air Force for air photography. I should like to know how much is spent on each part; whether or not this commercial work has been let by tender to commercial companies; and whether these photographs, when they are finished, are available to commercial companies, we will say, for surveying tinfiber limits.

I have not the exact figures before me, because the contracts have not all been let for this year. But the proportion will be about three to one; that is, three in favour of the R.C.A.F. to one in favour of the commercial companies. The work done by commercial companies is all let by tender. What was the other question?
The amount to defray expenses of the inter-departmental committee on air surveys.
I am told that is a small item, practically nothing.
